U.S. EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY COMMISSION
Office of Federal Operations
P.O. Box 77960
Washington, DC 20013

Herta R.,
1
Complainant,

v.

Sonny Perdue,
Secretary,
Department of Agriculture
(Food and Nutrition Service),
Agency.

Appeal No. 0120182270

Agency No. FNCS201700605

DECISION

On June 30, 2018, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
June 12, 2018, final decision concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) compl aint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq., and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the following reasons,
the Commission VACATES the Agency’s final decision , and REMANDS her complaint for
further processing in accordance with the ORDER below.

ISSUE PRESENTED

Whether the Agency’s final decision should be vacated because the Agency failed to provide
Complainant with a copy of its Report of Investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to select an
administrative hearing or a final decision.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 0120182270

2
BACKGROUND

The record reveals that, during the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Nutritionist, GS-0630-
13, at the Agency’s fa cility in Alexandria, Virginia. O n August 18, 2017, Complainant filed an
EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated and harassed her on the bases of sex
(female), color (black), disability (femoroacetabular impingement with labral tearing), age (43),
and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity with respect to six (6) issues. She alleged that:

1. On December 8, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Counseling and accused
her of lying about her disability to avoid work;
2. On October 30, 2017, management issued her 2017 performance appraisal , which
contained exaggerated and/or false statements, and thereafter on December 1, 2017,
denied her appeal of said performance appraisal;
3. On May 5, 2017, management denied her request for ad hoc telework;
4. On April 4, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Record accusing her of using
dates of unscheduled leave;
5. On an unspecified date, management forced her to share her medical condition to
the entire staff via email;
6. On several unspecified dates, she was subjected to various incidents of harassment,
including but not limited to:
a. On an unspecified date, management made false statements about her work
performance and work product;
b. On an unspecified date, management purposely misrepresented the Alternative
Dispute Resolution process to her; and
c. On an unspecified date, bulky pieces of furniture were purposely set in place to
block her cubical, which impeded her walkway.

According to the Agency, at the end of the investigation, Complainant , in March 2018, was
provided a copy of the investigative file and was informed of her right to request a hearing before
an EEOC Administrative Judge, or alternatively to receive a final decision by the Agency. When
Complainant, according to the Agency, did not request a hearing within the time frame provided
in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.110(b).
The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to
discrimination as alleged. This appeal followed.

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends, in pertinent part, that she did not receive the ROI nor notice of
her option to select an administrative hearing or a final decision. According to Complainant, she
repeatedly notified the Agency that she had moved, but that the Agency continued mailing
documents to her old address.

The Agency did not provide a statement on appeal.

 0120182270

3
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R §1614.108 (f) provides, in pertinent part, that the agency shall provide
the complainant with a copy of the investigative file, and shall notify the complainant that, within
30 days of receipt of the investigative file, the complainant has the right to request a hearing and
decision from an administrative judge or may request an immediate final decision pursuant to §
1614.110 from the agency with which the complaint was filed.

On appeal, Complainant stated that:

I did not receive a letter . . . to elect an EEOC hearing or final agency decision [n]or
have I received the Report of Investigation after several attempts to get a copy. The
Agency purposely and repeatedly sent correspondence to the wrong address after
several corrections I sent informing them they were sending correspondence to the
wrong address. The final agency decision included in this appeal was even sent to
the wrong address on June 13, 2018, which I did not receive until June 29, 2018.

The record contains a January 19, 2018, email from Complainant to A1, the Chief, Employment
Complaints Division, where she stated, among other things, “ Hello - I received the letter of
acceptance dated 12/22/17. The information regarding my claim is incorrect. In addition, the
communication was again sent to the wrong address, which caused a delay in receiving the letter,
which was received this week.”

A May 11, 2018, email from an EEO Specialist to Complainant states that: “On March 27, 2018,
we distributed your RO I to an address identified on several correspondence letters in your case
file. UPS notes that a person name [Complainant’s last name] signed for the document. Can you
please confirm if you received the document?”

On May 14, 2018, Complainant responded that: “I never received the report of investigation. My
address is [her new address was provided]. I corrected the address multiple times with [A1] Will
it be traced to determine who has the ROI as there is protected medical information about me in
that ROI?”

On May 31, 2018, Complainant wrote the Agency that:

Communication from the Agency has been repeatedly sent to the wrong address
after several attempts of updating my address. Most recently, the Report of
Investigation with my protected medical informa tion, was sent to my previous
address and the current tenants are refusing to acknowledge they have the material.

Notwithstanding the above, the Agency’s June 12, 2018, final decision was also sent to
Complainant’s previous address not her current address.
The Agency did not directly respond to these assertions by Complainant either on appeal or in the
record.

 0120182270

4
We do note that the record does contain an UPS receipt indicating that a 5 -pound package was
received at Complainant’s prior address on March 28, 2018 and signed for by someone with
Complainant’s last name.
2 There was no first name provided, nor was the actual signature
provided. Consequently, in light of Complainant’s undisputed evidence that as early as January
2018, she informed the Agency that it was sending documents to the wrong address , we are not
persuaded that the information sent to her previous address and signed for by someone writing her
last name was received by Complainant.

Based on our review of the record, we find it reasonable to conclude that the Agency, after being
informed of Complainant’s new address, repeatedly failed to update its records and sent documents
pertaining to her complaint to the wrong address, i.e., her previous address. The UPS receipt,
provided by the Agency, indicates that the ROI and notice were sent to her previous address. After
being notified of this error on May 14, 2018, and that Complainant stated that she never received
copies of these documents, the record is silent as to any corrective action taken by the Agency.
Accordingly, we find that Complainant satisfied her burden to keep the A gency abreast of her
proper address, and that the Agency did not comply with 29 C.F.R. §1614.108(f), to ensure that
both a copy of the investigative file and notification of the right to request a hearing was furnished
to Complainant.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, the Agency's final decision is VACATED. The complaint is hereby REMANDED
to the Agency for further processing in accordance with this decision and the Order below.

ORDER

The Agency, within thirty (30) calendar days of its receipt of this decision, shall send to
Complainant, at her current address, the Report of Investigation, and notice of her rights.
The Agency shall notify Complainant that within thirty (30) calendar days of her receipt of
the Report of Investigation and notice of her rights that she has the right to request a hearing
and a d ecision from an EEOC Administrative Judge or may request a n immediate final
decision from the Agency pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110. The Agency shall issue a
compliance report as referenced immediately below. This report must include a copy of
Complainant’s request for a hearing or a final decision.

2 We note that although Complainant’s uses a hyphenated last name, the UPS receipt was signed
by someone using only one of her names.

 0120182270

5
IMPLEMENTATION OF THE COMMISSION’S DECISION (K0719)
Under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c) and § 1614.502, compliance with the Commission’s corrective
action is mandatory. Within seven (7) calendar days of the completion of each ordered corrective
action, the Agency shall submit via the Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP) supporting documents
in the digital format required by the Commission, referencing the compliance docket number under
which compliance was being monitored. Once all compliance is complete, the Age ncy shall
submit via FedSEP a final compliance report in the digital format required by the Commission.
See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). The Agency’s final report must contain supporting documentation
when previously not uploaded, and the Agency must send a copy of all submissions to the
Complainant and his/her representative.
If the Agency does not comply with the Commission’s order, the Complainant may petition the
Commission for enforcement of the order. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(a). The Complainant also ha s
the right to file a civil action to enforce compliance with the Commission’s order prior to or
following an administrative petition for enforcement. See 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.407, 1614.408, and
29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(g). Alternatively, the Complainant has the right to file a civil action on the
underlying complaint in accordance with the paragraph below entitled “Right to File a Civil
Action.” 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.407 and 1614.408. A civil action for enforcement or a civil action on
the underlying complaint is subject to the deadline stated in 42 U.S.C. 2000e-16(c) (1994 & Supp.
IV 1999). If the Complainant files a civil action, the administrative processing of the
complaint, including any petition for enforcement, will be terminated. See 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.409.
Failure by an agency to either file a compliance report or implement any of the orders set forth in
this decision, without good cause shown, may result in the referral of this matter to the Office of
Special Counsel pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(f) for enforcement by that agency.
STATEMENT OF RIGHTS - ON APPEAL
RECONSIDERATION (M0617)
The Commission may, in its discretion, reconsider the decision in this case if the Complainant or
the Agency submits a written request containing arguments or evidence which tend to establish
that:
1. The appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or
law; or
2. The appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or
operations of the Agency.
Requests to reconsider, with supporting statement or brief, must be filed with the Office of Federal
Operations (OFO) within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of this decision. A party shall have
twenty (20) calendar days of receipt of another party’s time ly request for reconsideration in
which to submit a brief or statement in opposition.

 0120182270

6
See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405; Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R.
Part 1614 (EEO MD-110), at Chap. 9 § VII.B (Aug. 5, 2015). All requests and arguments must
be submitted to the Director, Office of Federal Operations, Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission. Complainant’s request may be submitted via regular mail to P.O. Box 77960,
Washington, DC 20013, or by certified mail to 131 M Street, NE, Washington, DC 20507. In the
absence of a legible postmark, the request to reconsider shall be deemed timely filed if it is received
by mail within five days of the expiration of the applicable filing period. See 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.604. The agency’s request must be submitted in digital format via the EEOC’s Federal
Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP). See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). The request or opposition must also
include proof of service on the other party.
Failure to file within the time period will result in dismissal of your request for reconsideration as
untimely, unless extenuating circumstances prevented the timely filing of the request. Any
supporting documentation must be submitted with your request for reconsideration. The
Commission will consider requests for reconsideration filed after the deadline only in very limited
circumstances. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(c).
COMPLAINANT’S RIGHT TO FILE A CIVIL ACTION (R0610)
This is a decision requiring the Agency to continue its administrative processing of your complaint.
However, if you wish to file a civil action, you have the right to file such action in an appropriate
United States District Court within ninety (90) calendar days from the date that you receive this
decision. In the alternative, you may file a civil action after one hundred and eighty (180)
calendar days of the date you filed your complaint with the Agency or filed your appeal with the
Commission. If you file a civil action, you must name as the defendant in the complaint the person
who is the official Agency head or department head, identifying that person by his or her full name
and official title. Failure to do so may result in the dismissal of your c ase in court. “Agency” or
“department” means the national organization, and not the local office, facility or department in
which you work. Filing a civil action will terminate the administrative processing of your
complaint.
RIGHT TO REQUEST COUNSEL (Z0815)
If you want to file a civil action but cannot pay the fees, costs, or security to do so, you may request
permission from the court to proceed with the civil action without paying these fees or costs.
Similarly, if you cannot afford an attorney to represent you in the civil action, you may request the
court to appoint an attorney for you. You must submit the requests for waiver of court costs or
appointment of an attorney directly to the court, not the Commission. The court has the sole
discretion to grant or deny these types of requests.

 0120182270

7
Such requests do not alter the time limits for filing a civil action (please read the paragraph titled
Complainant’s Right to File a Civil Action for the specific time limits).
FOR THE COMMISSION:

______________________________ Carlton M. Hadden’s signature
Carlton M. Hadden, Director
Office of Federal Operations

December 11, 2019
Date

U.S. EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY COMMISSION
Office of Federal Operations
P.O. Box 77960
Washington, DC 20013

Herta R.,
1
Complainant,

v.

Sonny Perdue,
Secretary,
Department of Agriculture
(Food and Nutrition Service),
Agency.

Appeal No. 0120182270

Agency No. FNCS201700605

DECISION

On June 30, 2018, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
June 12, 2018, final decision concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) compl aint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq., and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the following reasons,
the Commission VACATES the Agency’s final decision , and REMANDS her complaint for
further processing in accordance with the ORDER below.

ISSUE PRESENTED

Whether the Agency’s final decision should be vacated because the Agency failed to provide
Complainant with a copy of its Report of Investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to select an
administrative hearing or a final decision.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 0120182270

2
BACKGROUND

The record reveals that, during the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Nutritionist, GS-0630-
13, at the Agency’s fa cility in Alexandria, Virginia. O n August 18, 2017, Complainant filed an
EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated and harassed her on the bases of sex
(female), color (black), disability (femoroacetabular impingement with labral tearing), age (43),
and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity with respect to six (6) issues. She alleged that:

1. On December 8, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Counseling and accused
her of lying about her disability to avoid work;
2. On October 30, 2017, management issued her 2017 performance appraisal , which
contained exaggerated and/or false statements, and thereafter on December 1, 2017,
denied her appeal of said performance appraisal;
3. On May 5, 2017, management denied her request for ad hoc telework;
4. On April 4, 2017, management issued her a Letter of Record accusing her of using
dates of unscheduled leave;
5. On an unspecified date, management forced her to share her medical condition to
the entire staff via email;
6. On several unspecified dates, she was subjected to various incidents of harassment,
including but not limited to:
a. On an unspecified date, management made false statements about her work
performance and work product;
b. On an unspecified date, management purposely misrepresented the Alternative
Dispute Resolution process to her; and
c. On an unspecified date, bulky pieces of furniture were purposely set in place to
block her cubical, which impeded her walkway.

According to the Agency, at the end of the investigation, Complainant , in March 2018, was
provided a copy of the investigative file and was informed of her right to request a hearing before
an EEOC Administrative Judge, or alternatively to receive a final decision by the Agency. When
Complainant, according to the Agency, did not request a hearing within the time frame provided
in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §1614.110(b).
The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to
discrimination as alleged. This appeal followed.

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends, in pertinent part, that she did not receive the ROI nor notice of
her option to select an administrative hearing or a final decision. According to Complainant, she
repeatedly notified the Agency that she had moved, but that the Agency continued mailing
documents to her old address.

The Agency did not provide a statement on appeal.

 0120182270

3
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R §1614.108 (f) provides, in pertinent part, that the agency shall provide
the complainant with a copy of the investigative file, and shall notify the complainant that, within
30 days of receipt of the investigative file, the complainant has the right to request a hearing and
decision from an administrative judge or may request an immediate final decision pursuant to §
1614.110 from the agency with which the complaint was filed.

On appeal, Complainant stated that:

I did not receive a letter . . . to elect an EEOC hearing or final agency decision [n]or
have I received the Report of Investigation after several attempts to get a copy. The
Agency purposely and repeatedly sent correspondence to the wrong address after
several corrections I sent informing them they were sending correspondence to the
wrong address. The final agency decision included in this appeal was even sent to
the wrong address on June 13, 2018, which I did not receive until June 29, 2018.

The record contains a January 19, 2018, email from Complainant to A1, the Chief, Employment
Complaints Division, where she stated, among other things, “ Hello - I received the letter of
acceptance dated 12/22/17. The information regarding my claim is incorrect. In addition, the
communication was again sent to the wrong address, which caused a delay in receiving the letter,
which was received this week.”

A May 11, 2018, email from an EEO Specialist to Complainant states that: “On March 27, 2018,
we distributed your RO I to an address identified on several correspondence letters in your case
file. UPS notes that a person name [Complainant’s last name] signed for the document. Can you
please confirm if you received the document?”

On May 14, 2018, Complainant responded that: “I never received the report of investigation. My
address is [her new address was provided]. I corrected the address multiple times with [A1] Will
it be traced to determine who has the ROI as there is protected medical information about me in
that ROI?”

On May 31, 2018, Complainant wrote the Agency that:

Communication from the Agency has been repeatedly sent to the wrong address
after several attempts of updating my address. Most recently, the Report of
Investigation with my protected medical informa tion, was sent to my previous
address and the current tenants are refusing to acknowledge they have the material.

Notwithstanding the above, the Agency’s June 12, 2018, final decision was also sent to
Complainant’s previous address not her current address.
The Agency did not directly respond to these assertions by Complainant either on appeal or in the
record.

 0120182270

4
We do note that the record does contain an UPS receipt indicating that a 5 -pound package was
received at Complainant’s prior address on March 28, 2018 and signed for by someone with
Complainant’s last name.
2 There was no first name provided, nor was the actual signature
provided. Consequently, in light of Complainant’s undisputed evidence that as early as January
2018, she informed the Agency that it was sending documents to the wrong address , we are not
persuaded that the information sent to her previous address and signed for by someone writing her
last name was received by Complainant.

Based on our review of the record, we find it reasonable to conclude that the Agency, after being
informed of Complainant’s new address, repeatedly failed to update its records and sent documents
pertaining to her complaint to the wrong address, i.e., her previous address. The UPS receipt,
provided by the Agency, indicates that the ROI and notice were sent to her previous address. After
being notified of this error on May 14, 2018, and that Complainant stated that she never received
copies of these documents, the record is silent as to any corrective action taken by the Agency.
Accordingly, we find that Complainant satisfied her burden to keep the A gency abreast of her
proper address, and that the Agency did not comply with 29 C.F.R. §1614.108(f), to ensure that
both a copy of the investigative file and notification of the right to request a hearing was furnished
to Complainant.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, the Agency's final decision is VACATED. The complaint is hereby REMANDED
to the Agency for further processing in accordance with this decision and the Order below.

ORDER

The Agency, within thirty (30) calendar days of its receipt of this decision, shall send to
Complainant, at her current address, the Report of Investigation, and notice of her rights.
The Agency shall notify Complainant that within thirty (30) calendar days of her receipt of
the Report of Investigation and notice of her rights that she has the right to request a hearing
and a d ecision from an EEOC Administrative Judge or may request a n immediate final
decision from the Agency pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110. The Agency shall issue a
compliance report as referenced immediately below. This report must include a copy of
Complainant’s request for a hearing or a final decision.

2 We note that although Complainant’s uses a hyphenated last name, the UPS receipt was signed
by someone using only one of her names.

 0120182270

5
IMPLEMENTATION OF THE COMMISSION’S DECISION (K0719)
Under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c) and § 1614.502, compliance with the Commission’s corrective
action is mandatory. Within seven (7) calendar days of the completion of each ordered corrective
action, the Agency shall submit via the Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP) supporting documents
in the digital format required by the Commission, referencing the compliance docket number under
which compliance was being monitored. Once all compliance is complete, the Age ncy shall
submit via FedSEP a final compliance report in the digital format required by the Commission.
See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). The Agency’s final report must contain supporting documentation
when previously not uploaded, and the Agency must send a copy of all submissions to the
Complainant and his/her representative.
If the Agency does not comply with the Commission’s order, the Complainant may petition the
Commission for enforcement of the order. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(a). The Complainant also ha s
the right to file a civil action to enforce compliance with the Commission’s order prior to or
following an administrative petition for enforcement. See 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.407, 1614.408, and
29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(g). Alternatively, the Complainant has the right to file a civil action on the
underlying complaint in accordance with the paragraph below entitled “Right to File a Civil
Action.” 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.407 and 1614.408. A civil action for enforcement or a civil action on
the underlying complaint is subject to the deadline stated in 42 U.S.C. 2000e-16(c) (1994 & Supp.
IV 1999). If the Complainant files a civil action, the administrative processing of the
complaint, including any petition for enforcement, will be terminated. See 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.409.
Failure by an agency to either file a compliance report or implement any of the orders set forth in
this decision, without good cause shown, may result in the referral of this matter to the Office of
Special Counsel pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(f) for enforcement by that agency.
STATEMENT OF RIGHTS - ON APPEAL
RECONSIDERATION (M0617)
The Commission may, in its discretion, reconsider the decision in this case if the Complainant or
the Agency submits a written request containing arguments or evidence which tend to establish
that:
1. The appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or
law; or
2. The appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or
operations of the Agency.
Requests to reconsider, with supporting statement or brief, must be filed with the Office of Federal
Operations (OFO) within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of this decision. A party shall have
twenty (20) calendar days of receipt of another party’s time ly request for reconsideration in
which to submit a brief or statement in opposition.

 0120182270

6
See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405; Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R.
Part 1614 (EEO MD-110), at Chap. 9 § VII.B (Aug. 5, 2015). All requests and arguments must
be submitted to the Director, Office of Federal Operations, Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission. Complainant’s request may be submitted via regular mail to P.O. Box 77960,
Washington, DC 20013, or by certified mail to 131 M Street, NE, Washington, DC 20507. In the
absence of a legible postmark, the request to reconsider shall be deemed timely filed if it is received
by mail within five days of the expiration of the applicable filing period. See 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.604. The agency’s request must be submitted in digital format via the EEOC’s Federal
Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP). See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). The request or opposition must also
include proof of service on the other party.
Failure to file within the time period will result in dismissal of your request for reconsideration as
untimely, unless extenuating circumstances prevented the timely filing of the request. Any
supporting documentation must be submitted with your request for reconsideration. The
Commission will consider requests for reconsideration filed after the deadline only in very limited
circumstances. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(c).
COMPLAINANT’S RIGHT TO FILE A CIVIL ACTION (R0610)
This is a decision requiring the Agency to continue its administrative processing of your complaint.
However, if you wish to file a civil action, you have the right to file such action in an appropriate
United States District Court within ninety (90) calendar days from the date that you receive this
decision. In the alternative, you may file a civil action after one hundred and eighty (180)
calendar days of the date you filed your complaint with the Agency or filed your appeal with the
Commission. If you file a civil action, you must name as the defendant in the complaint the person
who is the official Agency head or department head, identifying that person by his or her full name
and official title. Failure to do so may result in the dismissal of your c ase in court. “Agency” or
“department” means the national organization, and not the local office, facility or department in
which you work. Filing a civil action will terminate the administrative processing of your
complaint.
RIGHT TO REQUEST COUNSEL (Z0815)
If you want to file a civil action but cannot pay the fees, costs, or security to do so, you may request
permission from the court to proceed with the civil action without paying these fees or costs.
Similarly, if you cannot afford an attorney to represent you in the civil action, you may request the
court to appoint an attorney for you. You must submit the requests for waiver of court costs or
appointment of an attorney directly to the court, not the Commission. The court has the sole
discretion to grant or deny these types of requests.

 0120182270

7
Such requests do not alter the time limits for filing a civil action (please read the paragraph titled
Complainant’s Right to File a Civil Action for the specific time limits).

U.S. EQUAL EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITY COMMISSION
Office of Federal Operations
P.O. Box 77960
Washington, DC 20013

Susann G.,
1
Complainant,

v.

Robert Wilkie,
Secretary,
Department of Veterans Affairs,
Agency.

Appeal No. 2019001984

Agency No. 200I-0516-2015102375

DECISION

On December 7, 2018, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
November 16, 2018 final decision concerning an equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. The Commission accepts the appeal in accordance
with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405.

BACKGROUND

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Medical Support Assistant (MSA), GS -5, at
the Agency’s Bay Pines Medical Center in Bay Pines, Florida.

In 2013, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that her supervisor was sexually harassing
her. The supervisor was subsequently terminated in July 2014. However, in December 2014, the
supervisor returned to the facility on numerous occasions. Due to the ex -supervisor’s presence,
Complainant requested a reassignment to another MSA position, one where her ex-supervisor
would not have access. Before being transferred, Complainant was informed that she was eligible
for an upcoming non- competitive promotion to GS -6 MSA. In meeting with management
regarding the move, she confirmed her eligibility for the promotion to GS -6. Complainant’s
transfer was approved and effective December 29, 2014.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2019001984

2
In late February 2015, management issued a memorandum identifying the individuals who had
been referred to Human Resources for the promotion. When Complainant asked why she was not
included, the Agency explained that her current work in an inpatient area did not qualify.

Believing that the Agency’s failure to promot e her was reprisal for her prior EEO activity,
Complainant filed an EEO complaint on April 27, 2017. Complainant requested a hearing before
an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ), but later withdrew her request. The case was remanded to
the Agency, which issued a decision finding no discrimination. Complainant appealed the decision
to the Commission.

In Complainant v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 0120162437 (May 25, 2018), the
Commission found the record contained evidence of pretext. T he Agency explained that
Complainant was not promoted to GS -6 simply because her requested transfer was granted and
she was placed in a position that was n ot eligible for the promotion. However the record
established that when Complainant requested the move, she also inquired about maintaining her
eligibility for the upcoming promotion. See id. In response, the management official told
Complainant that she would be moved to a position that allowed for the promotion to GS -6,
because she was already in such a position. See id. Following th is initial meeting with
Complainant and her union representative, the management official purportedly met with two other
managers. See id. The Commission observed that the record did not contain any information
regarding the content of the subsequent meeting/s or information on what positions were available.
See id. Moreover, management did not inform Complainant that her new position was ineligible
for the promotion and Complainant’s SF -50 was never updated to reflect the move. See id. The
Commission concluded that “due to the Agency’s actions, Complainant received a significantly
less desirable reassignment after a report of harassment which the Agency does not dispute
occurred.” See id. The Agency was ordered to offer Complainant the promotion, provide back pay,
consider compensatory damages, and train the responsible managers on their EEO obligations.
Additionally, Complainant was entitled to attorney’s fees and costs.

Complainant filed a request for reconsideration of the decision, limited to the matter of leave
restoration. See Complainant v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs , EEOC Request No. 05201800483
(September 27, 2018). The request was denied. T he Commission explained that the previous
order instructed the Agency to calculate Complainant’s entitleme nt to “back pay and benefits ,”
which encompassed leave. Nevertheless, the Commission issued a new order, modifying the order
in EEOC Appeal No. 0120162437, for clarity. Complainant was expressly provided the
opportunity to offer evidence regarding lost leave. See id.

On August 13, 2018, Complainant’s attorney requested the Agency pay $35,862.85 for 101.3 hours
of work at a rate of $350 per hour, as well as $407.85 in costs. The request was comprised of three
petitions: the “Initial Petition”, for 60 hou rs completed between December 8, 2015 and June 4,
2018; “Second Petition”, for 19 hours expended from June 6 through June 29, 2018, on the matter
of compensatory damages; and “Third Petition” for 22.3 hours worked between June 24, 2018 and
August 2, 2018, on the request for reconsideration and compensatory damages.

 2019001984

3
In a decision dated November 16, 2018
2, the Agency concluded that Complainant was only entitled
to 47.8 hours ($16,730.00) and $302.83 in costs. The record reflects that, on November 30, 2018,
the Agency issued a check payable to Complainant’s attorney in the amount of $17,032.83.

As an initial matter, the Agency accepted Complainant’s attorney’s hourly rate ($350) and agreed
that Complainant was a “prevailing party ,” with respect to the finding of discrimination. The
Agency, however, disagreed with the number of hours claimed by Complainant. The Agency
excluded hours in three categories it labeled : “Non-productive Efforts”; “Not Prevailing Party”;
and “Compensatory Damages”. The Agency determined that 37.6 hours expended on a hearing,
that was later withdrawn by Complainant, were not productive or reimbursable. This included
time spent on client conferences, discovery responses, and calls with opposing counsel. Because
Complainant’s request for reconsideration (EEOC Request No. 0520180482) was denied, the
Agency found that Complainant was not a “prevailing party” and not eligible for the 13.2 hours
spent on the request. Finally, with respect to compensatory damages
3, the Agency observed that
Complainant’s attorney sought 2.7 hours purportedly conducting research for compensatory
damages, on July 18, 2018, when the petition was submitted on June 25, 2018.

Complainant filed the instant appeal.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Title VII and the Commission's regulations authorize the award of reasonable attorney's fees and
costs to a prevailing complainant. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.501(e); see also EEO Management Directive
for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110), at 11-1 (Aug. 5, 2015). Fee awards are typically calculated
by multiplying the number of hours reasonably expended times a reasonable hourly rate, an amount
also known as a lodestar. See 29 C.F.R. §1614.501(e)(ii)(B); Blum v. Stenson, 465 U.S. 886, 899
(1984); Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424, 435 (1983).

All hours reasonably spent in processing the complaint are compensable, but the number of hours
should not include excessive, redundant or otherwise unnecessary hours. EEO MD -110 at 11-15.
A reasonable hourly rate is based on prevailing market rates in the relevant community for
attorneys of similar experience in similar cases. Id. at 11-6. An application for attorney's fees must
include a verified statement of attorney's fees accompanied by an affidavit executed by the attorney
of record itemizing the attorney's charges for legal services. Id. at 11-9.

While an attorney is not required to record in detail the way each minute of his or her time was
expended, the attorney does have the burden of identifying the subject matters on which he or she
spent his or her time by submitting sufficiently detailed and contemporaneous time records to

2 On the same date, the Agency issued a separate decision regarding compensatory damages.

3 The Agency also discussed 12.1 hours (Petition- 1) and 14.8 hours (Petition- 2) expended on
preparing and drafting the request for compensator y damages but the hours were not included in
the deductions.

 2019001984

4
ensure that the time spent was accurately recorded. See Complainant v. Dep't of the Treasury ,
EEOC Appeal No. 07A10035 (May 6, 2003). The attorney requesting the fee award has the burden
of proving, by specific evidence, entitlement to the requested fees and costs. Complainant v. U.S.
Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05A20843 (Feb. 18, 2003).

 Hourly Rate

As stated in its decision, the Agency does not challenge the reasonableness of the requested hourly
rate of $350/hour.

 Hours Expended

As noted above, the Agency deducted the hours related to work completed while the matter was
pending before an EEOC AJ because the hearing request was subsequently withdrawn.
Complainant’s attorney argues on appeal that the “time expended in discovery pri or to hearing
were essential to the prosecution of [Complainant’s] claims.” Specifically, he explains that a
hearing was requested because the report of investigation was incomplete. Complainant found
that a fter the parties “engaged in extensive written discovery ,” the Agency’s responses were
“sufficient to complete the investigation.” According to Complainant, the subsequent Commission
decision in her favor cited discovery information, illustrating that the evidence gathered during
the, albeit incomplete hearing stage was important to her eventual success.

The Agency does not dispute the deficiency of the report of investigation or the reliance on
information gathered at the hearing stage in the ultimate finding of discrimination. Therefore, we
find that it is reasonable to include the hours spent before the AJ in Complainant’s fee request.
The Agency erred in deducting the 37.6 hours expended by the attorney at the hearing stage.

The Agency found that 13.2 hours applied to work on Complainant’s request for reconsideration
should be excluded because the request was ultimately denied by the Commission. T he Agency
acknowledged that the decision did, in a sense, “reopen” the underlying case by explicitly
clarifying the equitable relief previously awarded. However, the Agency asserted that the decision
did not “confer any actual benefit or relief, as compared to Complainant’s initial condition prior
to the Motion for Reconsideration.” The Commission agrees. A prevailing party for this purpose
is one who succeeds on any significant issue, and achieves some of the benefit sought in bringing
the action. Davis v. Department of Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05970101 (February 4,
1999) (citing Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 427, 433 (1983)). Complainant did not achieve any
additional benefit as a result of filing her request for reconsideration, as her request was explicitly
denied. The additional order merely provided clarification , regarding confusion on the part of
Complainant’s counsel, by explaining that the previous award of remedies encompassed leave
reimbursement.
4

4 A review of the report of investigation conducted on compensatory damages (completed days
before our decision in EEOC Request No. 0520180483 (Sept. 27, 2018)), reflects that information

 2019001984

5
Finally, with regard to hours worked on July 18, 2018, the Agency contends 2.7 hours were
claimed for research on compensatory damages weeks after the request for compensatory damages
was submitted. The record reflects, however, that an additional affidavit and exhibits regarding
damages was provided in early August 2018. Therefore, the Agency’s deduction is not
substantiated.

Therefore, we find that of the 101.3 hours requested by Complainant’s attorney, the Agency
properly deducted 13.2 hours expended on the unsuccessful request for reconsideration.
Complainant is entitled to $30,835 (101.3 hrs. – 13.2 hours = 88.1 hours. $350/hr. x 88.1=
$30,835). The instant record contains evidence of payment to Complainant’s attorney for
$17,032.83 (47.8 hrs. x $350= $16,730 + $302.83 costs) made on November 30, 2018. The
Agency shall provide payment to Complainant’s attorney in the amount of the outstanding
attorney’s fees in the sum of $14,105.

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, we MODIFY the
Agency’s decision on attorney’s fees and costs. The matter is REMANDED to the Agency in
accordance with this decision and the ORDER below.

ORDER

Within 60 calendar days of the date this decision is issued, the Agency shall pay to Complainant’s
attorney the additional sum of $14,105

DECISION

On December 7, 2018, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
November 16, 2018 final decision concerning an equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. The Commission accepts the appeal in accordance
with 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405.

BACKGROUND

During the relevant time, Complainant worked as a Medical Support Assistant (MSA), GS -5, at
the Agency’s Bay Pines Medical Center in Bay Pines, Florida.

In 2013, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that her supervisor was sexually harassing
her. The supervisor was subsequently terminated in July 2014. However, in December 2014, the
supervisor returned to the facility on numerous occasions. Due to the ex -supervisor’s presence,
Complainant requested a reassignment to another MSA position, one where her ex-supervisor
would not have access. Before being transferred, Complainant was informed that she was eligible
for an upcoming non- competitive promotion to GS -6 MSA. In meeting with management
regarding the move, she confirmed her eligibility for the promotion to GS -6. Complainant’s
transfer was approved and effective December 29, 2014.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2019001984

2
In late February 2015, management issued a memorandum identifying the individuals who had
been referred to Human Resources for the promotion. When Complainant asked why she was not
included, the Agency explained that her current work in an inpatient area did not qualify.

Believing that the Agency’s failure to promot e her was reprisal for her prior EEO activity,
Complainant filed an EEO complaint on April 27, 2017. Complainant requested a hearing before
an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ), but later withdrew her request. The case was remanded to
the Agency, which issued a decision finding no discrimination. Complainant appealed the decision
to the Commission.

In Complainant v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 0120162437 (May 25, 2018), the
Commission found the record contained evidence of pretext. T he Agency explained that
Complainant was not promoted to GS -6 simply because her requested transfer was granted and
she was placed in a position that was n ot eligible for the promotion. However the record
established that when Complainant requested the move, she also inquired about maintaining her
eligibility for the upcoming promotion. See id. In response, the management official told
Complainant that she would be moved to a position that allowed for the promotion to GS -6,
because she was already in such a position. See id. Following th is initial meeting with
Complainant and her union representative, the management official purportedly met with two other
managers. See id. The Commission observed that the record did not contain any information
regarding the content of the subsequent meeting/s or information on what positions were available.
See id. Moreover, management did not inform Complainant that her new position was ineligible
for the promotion and Complainant’s SF -50 was never updated to reflect the move. See id. The
Commission concluded that “due to the Agency’s actions, Complainant received a significantly
less desirable reassignment after a report of harassment which the Agency does not dispute
occurred.” See id. The Agency was ordered to offer Complainant the promotion, provide back pay,
consider compensatory damages, and train the responsible managers on their EEO obligations.
Additionally, Complainant was entitled to attorney’s fees and costs.

Complainant filed a request for reconsideration of the decision, limited to the matter of leave
restoration. See Complainant v. Dep’t of Veterans Affairs , EEOC Request No. 05201800483
(September 27, 2018). The request was denied. T he Commission explained that the previous
order instructed the Agency to calculate Complainant’s entitleme nt to “back pay and benefits ,”
which encompassed leave. Nevertheless, the Commission issued a new order, modifying the order
in EEOC Appeal No. 0120162437, for clarity. Complainant was expressly provided the
opportunity to offer evidence regarding lost leave. See id.

of work at a rate of $350 per hour, as well as $407.85 in costs. The request was comprised of three
petitions: the “Initial Petition”, for 60 hou rs completed between December 8, 2015 and June 4,
2018; “Second Petition”, for 19 hours expended from June 6 through June 29, 2018, on the matter
of compensatory damages; and “Third Petition” for 22.3 hours worked between June 24, 2018 and
August 2, 2018, on the request for reconsideration and compensatory damages.

 2019001984

3
In a decision dated November 16, 2018
2, the Agency concluded that Complainant was only entitled
to 47.8 hours ($16,730.00) and $302.83 in costs. The record reflects that, on November 30, 2018,
the Agency issued a check payable to Complainant’s attorney in the amount of $17,032.83.

As an initial matter, the Agency accepted Complainant’s attorney’s hourly rate ($350) and agreed
that Complainant was a “prevailing party ,” with respect to the finding of discrimination. The
Agency, however, disagreed with the number of hours claimed by Complainant. The Agency
excluded hours in three categories it labeled : “Non-productive Efforts”; “Not Prevailing Party”;
and “Compensatory Damages”. The Agency determined that 37.6 hours expended on a hearing,
that was later withdrawn by Complainant, were not productive or reimbursable. This included
time spent on client conferences, discovery responses, and calls with opposing counsel. Because
Complainant’s request for reconsideration (EEOC Request No. 0520180482) was denied, the
Agency found that Complainant was not a “prevailing party” and not eligible for the 13.2 hours
spent on the request. Finally, with respect to compensatory damages
3, the Agency observed that
Complainant’s attorney sought 2.7 hours purportedly conducting research for compensatory
damages, on July 18, 2018, when the petition was submitted on June 25, 2018.

Complainant filed the instant appeal.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Title VII and the Commission's regulations authorize the award of reasonable attorney's fees and
costs to a prevailing complainant. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.501(e); see also EEO Management Directive
for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110), at 11-1 (Aug. 5, 2015). Fee awards are typically calculated
by multiplying the number of hours reasonably expended times a reasonable hourly rate, an amount
also known as a lodestar. See 29 C.F.R. §1614.501(e)(ii)(B); Blum v. Stenson, 465 U.S. 886, 899
(1984); Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424, 435 (1983).

All hours reasonably spent in processing the complaint are compensable, but the number of hours
should not include excessive, redundant or otherwise unnecessary hours. EEO MD -110 at 11-15.
A reasonable hourly rate is based on prevailing market rates in the relevant community for
attorneys of similar experience in similar cases. Id. at 11-6. An application for attorney's fees must
include a verified statement of attorney's fees accompanied by an affidavit executed by the attorney
of record itemizing the attorney's charges for legal services. Id. at 11-9.

While an attorney is not required to record in detail the way each minute of his or her time was
expended, the attorney does have the burden of identifying the subject matters on which he or she
spent his or her time by submitting sufficiently detailed and contemporaneous time records to

2 On the same date, the Agency issued a separate decision regarding compensatory damages.

3 The Agency also discussed 12.1 hours (Petition- 1) and 14.8 hours (Petition- 2) expended on
preparing and drafting the request for compensator y damages but the hours were not included in
the deductions.

 2019001984

4
ensure that the time spent was accurately recorded. See Complainant v. Dep't of the Treasury ,
EEOC Appeal No. 07A10035 (May 6, 2003). The attorney requesting the fee award has the burden
of proving, by specific evidence, entitlement to the requested fees and costs. Complainant v. U.S.
Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05A20843 (Feb. 18, 2003).

 Hourly Rate

As stated in its decision, the Agency does not challenge the reasonableness of the requested hourly
rate of $350/hour.

 Hours Expended

As noted above, the Agency deducted the hours related to work completed while the matter was
pending before an EEOC AJ because the hearing request was subsequently withdrawn.
Complainant’s attorney argues on appeal that the “time expended in discovery pri or to hearing
were essential to the prosecution of [Complainant’s] claims.” Specifically, he explains that a
hearing was requested because the report of investigation was incomplete. Complainant found
that a fter the parties “engaged in extensive written discovery ,” the Agency’s responses were
“sufficient to complete the investigation.” According to Complainant, the subsequent Commission
decision in her favor cited discovery information, illustrating that the evidence gathered during
the, albeit incomplete hearing stage was important to her eventual success.

The Agency does not dispute the deficiency of the report of investigation or the reliance on
information gathered at the hearing stage in the ultimate finding of discrimination. Therefore, we
find that it is reasonable to include the hours spent before the AJ in Complainant’s fee request.
The Agency erred in deducting the 37.6 hours expended by the attorney at the hearing stage.

The Agency found that 13.2 hours applied to work on Complainant’s request for reconsideration
should be excluded because the request was ultimately denied by the Commission. T he Agency
acknowledged that the decision did, in a sense, “reopen” the underlying case by explicitly
clarifying the equitable relief previously awarded. However, the Agency asserted that the decision
did not “confer any actual benefit or relief, as compared to Complainant’s initial condition prior
to the Motion for Reconsideration.” The Commission agrees. A prevailing party for this purpose
is one who succeeds on any significant issue, and achieves some of the benefit sought in bringing
the action. Davis v. Department of Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05970101 (February 4,
1999) (citing Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 427, 433 (1983)). Complainant did not achieve any
additional benefit as a result of filing her request for reconsideration, as her request was explicitly
denied. The additional order merely provided clarification , regarding confusion on the part of
Complainant’s counsel, by explaining that the previous award of remedies encompassed leave
reimbursement.
4

4 A review of the report of investigation conducted on compensatory damages (completed days
before our decision in EEOC Request No. 0520180483 (Sept. 27, 2018)), reflects that information

 2019001984

5
Finally, with regard to hours worked on July 18, 2018, the Agency contends 2.7 hours were
claimed for research on compensatory damages weeks after the request for compensatory damages
was submitted. The record reflects, however, that an additional affidavit and exhibits regarding
damages was provided in early August 2018. Therefore, the Agency’s deduction is not
substantiated.

Therefore, we find that of the 101.3 hours requested by Complainant’s attorney, the Agency
properly deducted 13.2 hours expended on the unsuccessful request for reconsideration.
Complainant is entitled to $30,835 (101.3 hrs. – 13.2 hours = 88.1 hours. $350/hr. x 88.1=
$30,835). The instant record contains evidence of payment to Complainant’s attorney for
$17,032.83 (47.8 hrs. x $350= $16,730 + $302.83 costs) made on November 30, 2018. The
Agency shall provide payment to Complainant’s attorney in the amount of the outstanding
attorney’s fees in the sum of $14,105.

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, we MODIFY the
Agency’s decision on attorney’s fees and costs. The matter is REMANDED to the Agency in
accordance with this decision and the ORDER below.

(1984); Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424, 435 (1983).

All hours reasonably spent in processing the complaint are compensable, but the number of hours
should not include excessive, redundant or otherwise unnecessary hours. EEO MD -110 at 11-15.
A reasonable hourly rate is based on prevailing market rates in the relevant community for
attorneys of similar experience in similar cases. Id. at 11-6. An application for attorney's fees must
include a verified statement of attorney's fees accompanied by an affidavit executed by the attorney
of record itemizing the attorney's charges for legal services. Id. at 11-9.

While an attorney is not required to record in detail the way each minute of his or her time was
expended, the attorney does have the burden of identifying the subject matters on which he or she
spent his or her time by submitting sufficiently detailed and contemporaneous time records to

ensure that the time spent was accurately recorded. See Complainant v. Dep't of the Treasury ,

of proving, by specific evidence, entitlement to the requested fees and costs. Complainant v. U.S.
Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05A20843 (Feb. 18, 2003).

 Hourly Rate

As stated in its decision, the Agency does not challenge the reasonableness of the requested hourly
rate of $350/hour.

 Hours Expended

As noted above, the Agency deducted the hours related to work completed while the matter was
pending before an EEOC AJ because the hearing request was subsequently withdrawn.
Complainant’s attorney argues on appeal that the “time expended in discovery pri or to hearing
were essential to the prosecution of [Complainant’s] claims.” Specifically, he explains that a
hearing was requested because the report of investigation was incomplete. Complainant found
that a fter the parties “engaged in extensive written discovery ,” the Agency’s responses were
“sufficient to complete the investigation.” According to Complainant, the subsequent Commission
decision in her favor cited discovery information, illustrating that the evidence gathered during
the, albeit incomplete hearing stage was important to her eventual success.

The Agency does not dispute the deficiency of the report of investigation or the reliance on
information gathered at the hearing stage in the ultimate finding of discrimination. Therefore, we
find that it is reasonable to include the hours spent before the AJ in Complainant’s fee request.
The Agency erred in deducting the 37.6 hours expended by the attorney at the hearing stage.

The Agency found that 13.2 hours applied to work on Complainant’s request for reconsideration
should be excluded because the request was ultimately denied by the Commission. T he Agency
acknowledged that the decision did, in a sense, “reopen” the underlying case by explicitly
clarifying the equitable relief previously awarded. However, the Agency asserted that the decision
did not “confer any actual benefit or relief, as compared to Complainant’s initial condition prior
to the Motion for Reconsideration.” The Commission agrees. A prevailing party for this purpose
is one who succeeds on any significant issue, and achieves some of the benefit sought in bringing
the action. Davis v. Department of Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05970101 (February 4,
1999) (citing Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 427, 433 (1983)). Complainant did not achieve any
additional benefit as a result of filing her request for reconsideration, as her request was explicitly
denied. The additional order merely provided clarification , regarding confusion on the part of
Complainant’s counsel, by explaining that the previous award of remedies encompassed leave
reimbursement.
4

4 A review of the report of investigation conducted on compensatory damages (completed days

Finally, with regard to hours worked on July 18, 2018, the Agency contends 2.7 hours were
claimed for research on compensatory damages weeks after the request for compensatory damages
was submitted. The record reflects, however, that an additional affidavit and exhibits regarding
damages was provided in early August 2018. Therefore, the Agency’s deduction is not
substantiated.

Therefore, we find that of the 101.3 hours requested by Complainant’s attorney, the Agency
properly deducted 13.2 hours expended on the unsuccessful request for reconsideration.
Complainant is entitled to $30,835 (101.3 hrs. – 13.2 hours = 88.1 hours. $350/hr. x 88.1=

Agency shall provide payment to Complainant’s attorney in the amount of the outstanding
attorney’s fees in the sum of $14,105.

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, we MODIFY the
Agency’s decision on attorney’s fees and costs. The matter is REMANDED to the Agency in

DECISION

Complainant timely filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s November 21, 2018,
final decision concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging
employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII), as
amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq.

ISSUES PRESENTED

The issue presented is whether the Agency properly provided Complainant with the report of
investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing in accordance with 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.108(f).

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rural Carrier
Associate at the Agency’s Zephyrhills, Florida Post Office.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2019002184

2
On April 30, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated
against him on the bases of religion ( Christian), disability (FMLA/doctor appointments/entire
body), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
when:

1. On January 4, 2018, he was given an Investigative Interview and subsequently on
January 5, 2018, he was issued a Letter of Warning for Unsatisfactory Attendance;

2. Beginning on or about February 23, 2018, and continuing, he was required to work
on Sundays; and

3. On March 4, 2018, he was required to perform clerk duties and sort Amazon
parcels.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency sent Complainant a copy of the report of
investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission Administrative Judge via certified-mail, signature required. On October 30, 2018,
the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing were returned to the Agency. On
November 16, 2018, asserting that Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame
provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected
him to discrimination as alleged.

On December 19, 2018, Complainant simultaneously requested a hear ing and filed the instant
appeal.
2

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends that the Agency prematurely issued its final decision .
Complainant asserts that the Agency issued a final decision, dated November 21, 2018, prior to
his receipt of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing. Complainant
notes that he did not receive the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing until
December 13, 2018, at the request of his representative.

The Agency asserts that Complainant’s appeal should be denied because material facts are not in
dispute and Complainant failed to proffer evidence excusing his untimely hearing request. The
Agency adds that Complainant did not challenge any of the factual findings or conclusions of law
in the final decision.

2 On April 15, 2019, the assigned Administrative Judge issued an Order of Dismissal in response
to a Motion to Dismiss filed by the Agency on March 12, 2019. The Administrative Judge found
that Complainant could not pursue a hearing request at the same time as he pursued an appeal .
Accordingly, the hearing record was closed.

 2019002184

3
According to the Agency, five facts are dispositive of Complainant’s argument that he did not
receive the report of investigation and those facts establish the Agency’s due diligence in
delivering the report of investigation to Complainant. Specifically, the Agency states: (1) the
National EEO Investigative Services Office properly addressed the report of investigation and
mailed it to Complainant’s home of record; (2) delivery failed on September 13, 2018, and a postal
form notice was left on Complainant’s door; (3) the postal notice form apprised Complainant of
the attempted delivery and contained several convenient options for Complainant to claim the
report of investigation; (4) Complainant took no action to collect the report of investigation for 30
calendar days, despite having 10 days off during the period; and (5) after never receiving a hearing
election from Complainant, a final decision was issued. The Agency maintains that Complainant
received constructive notice of his right to request a hearing and his behavior does not establish
good cause for his 65-day untimely hearing request.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b),
the Agency's decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a).
See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614, at Chapter 9,
§ VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review “requires that the
Commission examine the record without regard to the factual and legal determinations of the
previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents, statements, and testimony of
record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the parties, and . . . issue its decision
based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and its interpretation of the law”).

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f) provides in relevant part that the agency shall provide
the complainant with a copy of the investigative file and shall notify the complainant that, within
30 days of receipt of the investigative file, the complainant has the right to request a hearing and
decision from an Administrative Judge or may request an immediate final decision pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.110 from the agency with which the complaint was filed.

Complainant, through counsel, maintains that he did not receive the report of investigation and
notice of the right to a hearing prior to the issuance of the final agency decision. Complainant
states that he was working at the time of the attempted delivery and did not learn that the report of
investigation was available until after he received the final agency decision, which was sent
without a required signature confirmation.

The Commission has vacated an agency’s final decision when the agency failed to provide
evidence that a complainant was in actual receipt of the investigative file and notice of right to
request a hearing. Hill v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01A60865 (May 12, 2006)
(complainant denied receiving the report of investigation and the Agency did not assert that the
complainant had been notified of the right to and/or the statutory time limit for requesting a
hearing).

 2019002184

4
Here, the Agency does not dispute that Complainant was not in receipt of the report of investigation
and notice of the right to request a hearing when it issued the final decision. Rather, the Agency
asserts that Complainant should have availed himself of his hearing rights. We disagree with the
Agency and find that the Agency failed to provide evidence that Complainant was in actual receipt
of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing prior to the issuance of the
final decision.

On appeal, the Agency argues that Complainant “constructively received the report of
investigation and adequate notice of his hearing rights on September 13, 2018 because he failed to
exercise any diligence to claim his report for 30 calendar days.” Citing Zemo v. Dep’ t of
Commerce, EEOC Appeal No. 01912813 (September 16, 1991) and Woehr v. U.S. Postal Service,
EEOC Request No. 05960657 (July 3, 1997), the Agency asserts that complainants have an
affirmative duty to exercise due diligence regarding the processing of their complaint.

In Zemo, supra, the agency sent a proposed disposition to the complainant’s home by certified
mail, which was returned unclaimed while the c omplainant was on vacation. The Agency also
sent the proposed disposition via regular mail, which was delivered to the complainant’s residence.
In finding that the complainant received constructive notice of the proposed disposition, t he
Commission noted that the complainant’s vacation was planned in advance and he could have
notified the agency of his whereabouts, provided an alternate address, designated a representative
to act on his behalf, or requested that the agency hold the processing of the claim in abeyance.

As for Woehr, supra, the Commission noted “[ the complainant] failed to act with due diligence
regarding his administrative rights. He filed his appeal with the Commission in October 1991 and
did not contact the Commission with a communication mentioning the appeal until May 1996.”
In Woehr, the Commission had attempted to provide the complainant with a copy of an appe llate
decision by mailing it to the complainant twice, resulting in six attempts to deliver the decision
over a two-month timespan, even though the decision was returned unclaimed. We find that the
instant matter does not involve facts analogous to Zemo or Woehr.

The Agency further cites Otterstedt v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01A05235 (March 19,
2002) for the proposition that a complainant is deemed to have constructively received documents
mailed to his last known address when he fails to notify the agency of an address change, yet there
is no dispute regarding Complainant’s address in this matter. The Agency contends that an on-
point appeal is Mazurek v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal Nos. 01A11033, 01995466 (January
23, 2002). We note, however, that in Mazurek , the Agency delivered the report of investigation
to the complainant’s post office box when certified -mail delivery failed , while delivery never
occurred in this instance.

We find the Agency’s argument that Complainant received constructive notice of his rights and
failed to act with due diligence unpersuasive. It is undisputed here that Complainant did not receive
a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing via certified mail or regular
mail prior to the issuance of the Agency’s final decision.

 2019002184

5
Moreover, Complainant immediately obtained legal counsel upon learning that procedural errors
existed, and Complainant’s counsel attempted to engage with the Agency regarding the errors .
The Agency has not demonstrated that Complainant was in actual receipt or had constructive
notice of the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing.

Further, to the extent the Agency asserts that Complainant filed an untimely hearin g request, we
note that the Commission has held that a complainant’s actual receipt of the notice of the right to
a hearing was necessary to commence the running of the time- limitation in which to request a
hearing. See Kellus v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05920198 (Apr. 20, 1992) (hearing
rights were sent certified mail and returned to the agency unclaimed and the agency failed to show
that the complainant actually received copies sent by regular mail) ; Battle v. U.S. Postal Serv.,
EEOC Request No. 05910441 (June 13, 1991) (complainant alleged that she did not receive a
proposed decision when certified mail was returned to the agency unclaimed, first -class mailing
was never returned, and the agency failed to provide evidence of proof of service).

Here, actual receipt of the investigative file did not occur until December 13, 2018, when the
Agency provided Complainant’s counsel with the investigative file. There is no evidence in the
record showing that Complainant received the report of investigation or notice of his right to a
hearing prior to this time , nor any indication in the record that the Agency made any additional
attempts to provide Complainant with the information after the certified mailing was returned. The
Agency provided an affidavit from the postal carrier who stated she left notice of the package.
However, Complainant stated that he received no such note. Contrary to the Agency’s assertion
that Complainant “at any time during the 30-calendar day period, could have requested redelivery
or designated someone to claim the report of investigation on his behalf,” the record does not
establish that Complainant had actual knowledge of the redelivery notice left at his door or the
contents of the undelivered package. Therefore, the Agency’s insinuation that Complainant sat on
his rights is purely speculative.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, we find Complainant filed a timely hearing request when he requested a hearing on
December 19, 2018. Therefore, based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on
appeal, including those not specifically addressed herein, we VACATE the Agency’s final
decision and REMAND the entire complaint in accordance with the Order below.
