DECISION

Complainant timely filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s November 21, 2018,
final decision concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging
employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII), as
amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., and Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq.

ISSUES PRESENTED

The issue presented is whether the Agency properly provided Complainant with the report of
investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing in accordance with 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.108(f).

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Rural Carrier
Associate at the Agency’s Zephyrhills, Florida Post Office.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2019002184

2
On April 30, 2018, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated
against him on the bases of religion ( Christian), disability (FMLA/doctor appointments/entire
body), and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
when:

1. On January 4, 2018, he was given an Investigative Interview and subsequently on
January 5, 2018, he was issued a Letter of Warning for Unsatisfactory Attendance;

2. Beginning on or about February 23, 2018, and continuing, he was required to work
on Sundays; and

3. On March 4, 2018, he was required to perform clerk duties and sort Amazon
parcels.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency sent Complainant a copy of the report of
investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission Administrative Judge via certified-mail, signature required. On October 30, 2018,
the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing were returned to the Agency. On
November 16, 2018, asserting that Complainant did not request a hearing within the time frame
provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected
him to discrimination as alleged.

On December 19, 2018, Complainant simultaneously requested a hear ing and filed the instant
appeal.
2

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends that the Agency prematurely issued its final decision .
Complainant asserts that the Agency issued a final decision, dated November 21, 2018, prior to
his receipt of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing. Complainant
notes that he did not receive the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing until
December 13, 2018, at the request of his representative.

The Agency asserts that Complainant’s appeal should be denied because material facts are not in
dispute and Complainant failed to proffer evidence excusing his untimely hearing request. The
Agency adds that Complainant did not challenge any of the factual findings or conclusions of law
in the final decision.

2 On April 15, 2019, the assigned Administrative Judge issued an Order of Dismissal in response
to a Motion to Dismiss filed by the Agency on March 12, 2019. The Administrative Judge found
that Complainant could not pursue a hearing request at the same time as he pursued an appeal .
Accordingly, the hearing record was closed.

 2019002184

3
According to the Agency, five facts are dispositive of Complainant’s argument that he did not
receive the report of investigation and those facts establish the Agency’s due diligence in
delivering the report of investigation to Complainant. Specifically, the Agency states: (1) the
National EEO Investigative Services Office properly addressed the report of investigation and
mailed it to Complainant’s home of record; (2) delivery failed on September 13, 2018, and a postal
form notice was left on Complainant’s door; (3) the postal notice form apprised Complainant of
the attempted delivery and contained several convenient options for Complainant to claim the
report of investigation; (4) Complainant took no action to collect the report of investigation for 30
calendar days, despite having 10 days off during the period; and (5) after never receiving a hearing
election from Complainant, a final decision was issued. The Agency maintains that Complainant
received constructive notice of his right to request a hearing and his behavior does not establish
good cause for his 65-day untimely hearing request.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b),
the Agency's decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a).
See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614, at Chapter 9,
§ VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review “requires that the
Commission examine the record without regard to the factual and legal determinations of the
previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents, statements, and testimony of
record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the parties, and . . . issue its decision
based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and its interpretation of the law”).

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f) provides in relevant part that the agency shall provide
the complainant with a copy of the investigative file and shall notify the complainant that, within
30 days of receipt of the investigative file, the complainant has the right to request a hearing and
decision from an Administrative Judge or may request an immediate final decision pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.110 from the agency with which the complaint was filed.

Complainant, through counsel, maintains that he did not receive the report of investigation and
notice of the right to a hearing prior to the issuance of the final agency decision. Complainant
states that he was working at the time of the attempted delivery and did not learn that the report of
investigation was available until after he received the final agency decision, which was sent
without a required signature confirmation.

The Commission has vacated an agency’s final decision when the agency failed to provide
evidence that a complainant was in actual receipt of the investigative file and notice of right to
request a hearing. Hill v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01A60865 (May 12, 2006)
(complainant denied receiving the report of investigation and the Agency did not assert that the
complainant had been notified of the right to and/or the statutory time limit for requesting a
hearing).

 2019002184

4
Here, the Agency does not dispute that Complainant was not in receipt of the report of investigation
and notice of the right to request a hearing when it issued the final decision. Rather, the Agency
asserts that Complainant should have availed himself of his hearing rights. We disagree with the
Agency and find that the Agency failed to provide evidence that Complainant was in actual receipt
of the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing prior to the issuance of the
final decision.

On appeal, the Agency argues that Complainant “constructively received the report of
investigation and adequate notice of his hearing rights on September 13, 2018 because he failed to
exercise any diligence to claim his report for 30 calendar days.” Citing Zemo v. Dep’ t of
Commerce, EEOC Appeal No. 01912813 (September 16, 1991) and Woehr v. U.S. Postal Service,
EEOC Request No. 05960657 (July 3, 1997), the Agency asserts that complainants have an
affirmative duty to exercise due diligence regarding the processing of their complaint.

In Zemo, supra, the agency sent a proposed disposition to the complainant’s home by certified
mail, which was returned unclaimed while the c omplainant was on vacation. The Agency also
sent the proposed disposition via regular mail, which was delivered to the complainant’s residence.
In finding that the complainant received constructive notice of the proposed disposition, t he
Commission noted that the complainant’s vacation was planned in advance and he could have
notified the agency of his whereabouts, provided an alternate address, designated a representative
to act on his behalf, or requested that the agency hold the processing of the claim in abeyance.

As for Woehr, supra, the Commission noted “[ the complainant] failed to act with due diligence
regarding his administrative rights. He filed his appeal with the Commission in October 1991 and
did not contact the Commission with a communication mentioning the appeal until May 1996.”
In Woehr, the Commission had attempted to provide the complainant with a copy of an appe llate
decision by mailing it to the complainant twice, resulting in six attempts to deliver the decision
over a two-month timespan, even though the decision was returned unclaimed. We find that the
instant matter does not involve facts analogous to Zemo or Woehr.

The Agency further cites Otterstedt v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01A05235 (March 19,
2002) for the proposition that a complainant is deemed to have constructively received documents
mailed to his last known address when he fails to notify the agency of an address change, yet there
is no dispute regarding Complainant’s address in this matter. The Agency contends that an on-
point appeal is Mazurek v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal Nos. 01A11033, 01995466 (January
23, 2002). We note, however, that in Mazurek , the Agency delivered the report of investigation
to the complainant’s post office box when certified -mail delivery failed , while delivery never
occurred in this instance.

We find the Agency’s argument that Complainant received constructive notice of his rights and
failed to act with due diligence unpersuasive. It is undisputed here that Complainant did not receive
a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing via certified mail or regular
mail prior to the issuance of the Agency’s final decision.

 2019002184

5
Moreover, Complainant immediately obtained legal counsel upon learning that procedural errors
existed, and Complainant’s counsel attempted to engage with the Agency regarding the errors .
The Agency has not demonstrated that Complainant was in actual receipt or had constructive
notice of the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing.

Further, to the extent the Agency asserts that Complainant filed an untimely hearin g request, we
note that the Commission has held that a complainant’s actual receipt of the notice of the right to
a hearing was necessary to commence the running of the time- limitation in which to request a
hearing. See Kellus v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05920198 (Apr. 20, 1992) (hearing
rights were sent certified mail and returned to the agency unclaimed and the agency failed to show
that the complainant actually received copies sent by regular mail) ; Battle v. U.S. Postal Serv.,
EEOC Request No. 05910441 (June 13, 1991) (complainant alleged that she did not receive a
proposed decision when certified mail was returned to the agency unclaimed, first -class mailing
was never returned, and the agency failed to provide evidence of proof of service).

Here, actual receipt of the investigative file did not occur until December 13, 2018, when the
Agency provided Complainant’s counsel with the investigative file. There is no evidence in the
record showing that Complainant received the report of investigation or notice of his right to a
hearing prior to this time , nor any indication in the record that the Agency made any additional
attempts to provide Complainant with the information after the certified mailing was returned. The
Agency provided an affidavit from the postal carrier who stated she left notice of the package.
However, Complainant stated that he received no such note. Contrary to the Agency’s assertion
that Complainant “at any time during the 30-calendar day period, could have requested redelivery
or designated someone to claim the report of investigation on his behalf,” the record does not
establish that Complainant had actual knowledge of the redelivery notice left at his door or the
contents of the undelivered package. Therefore, the Agency’s insinuation that Complainant sat on
his rights is purely speculative.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, we find Complainant filed a timely hearing request when he requested a hearing on
December 19, 2018. Therefore, based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on
appeal, including those not specifically addressed herein, we VACATE the Agency’s final
decision and REMAND the entire complaint in accordance with the Order below.

ORDER

The Agency is ordered to process the remanded claims in accordance with 29 C.F.R. §1614.109
et seq. Specifically, the Agency shall forward Complainant’s complaint file to an EEOC
Administrative Judge for scheduling of a hearing within fifteen (15) calendar days of the date this
decision becomes final. The Agency shall also acknowledge to Complainant that it has received
the remanded complaint within fifteen (15) calendar days of the date this decision becomes final.

 2019002184

6
A copy of the Agency’s letter of acknow ledgement to Complainant and a copy of the
correspondence that transmits the remanded complaint to the Administrative Judge must be sent
to the Compliance Officer as referenced below.
IMPLEMENTATION OF THE COMMISSION’S DECISION (K0719)
Under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c) and §1614.502, compliance with the Commission’s corrective
action is mandatory. Within seven (7) calendar days of the completion of each ordered corrective
action, the Agency shall submit via the Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP) supporting documents
in the digital format required by the Commission, referencing the compliance docket number under
which compliance was being monitored. Once all compliance is complete, the Agency shall
submit via FedSEP a final compliance report in the digital format required by the Commission.
See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). The Agency’s final report must contain supporting documentation
when previously not uploaded, and the Agency must send a copy of all submissions to the
Complainant and his/her representative.
If the Agency does not comply with the Commission’s order, the Complainant may petition the
Commission for enforcement of the order. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(a). The Complainant also has
the right to file a civil action to enforce compliance with the Commiss ion’s order prior to or
following an administrative petition for enforcement. See 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.407, 1614.408, and
29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(g). Alternatively, the Complainant has the right to file a civil action on the
underlying complaint in accordance with the paragraph below entitled “Right to File a Civil
Action.” 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.407 and 1614.408. A civil action for enforcement or a civil action on
the underlying complaint is subject to the deadline stated in 42 U.S.C. 2000e-16(c) (1994 & Supp.
IV 1999). If the Complainant files a civil action, the administrative processing of the
complaint, including any petition for enforcement, will be terminated. See 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.409.
Failure by an agency to either file a compliance report or implement an y of the orders set forth in
this decision, without good cause shown, may result in the referral of this matter to the Office of
Special Counsel pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.503(f) for enforcement by that agency.
STATEMENT OF RIGHTS - ON APPEAL
RECONSIDERATION (M0620)
The Commission may, in its discretion, reconsider this appellate decision if the complainant or the
agency submits a written request that contains arguments or evidence that tend to establish that:
1. The appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or
law; or
2. The appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or
operations of the agency.
Requests for reconsideration must be filed with EEOC’s Office of Federal Operations (OFO)
within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of this decision. If the party requesting reconsideration
elects to file a statement or brief in support of the request, that statement or brief must be filed
together with the request for reconsideration.

 2019002184

7
A party shall have twenty (20) calendar days from receipt of another party’s request for
reconsideration within which to submit a brief or statement in opposition. See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.405; Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO
MD-110), at Chap. 9 § VII.B (Aug. 5, 2015).
Complainant should submit his or her request for reconsideration, and any statement or brief in
support of his or her request, via the EEOC Public Portal, which can be found at
https://publicportal.eeoc.gov/Portal/Login.aspx.
Alternatively, complainant can submit his or her request and arguments to the Director, Office of
Federal Operations, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, via regular mail addressed to
P.O. Box 77960, Washington, DC 20013, or by certified mail addressed to 131 M Street, NE,
Washington, DC 20507. In the absence of a legible postmark, complainant’s request to reconsider
shall be deemed timely filed if OFO receives it by mail within five days of the expiration of the
applicable filing period. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604.
An agency’s request for reconsideration must be submitted in digital format via the EEOC’s
Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP). See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). Either party’s request and/or
statement or brief in opposition must also include proof of service on the other party, unless
complainant files his or her request via the EEOC Public Portal, in which case no proof of service
is required.
Failure to file within the 30-day time period will result in dismissal of the party’s request for
reconsideration as untimely, unless extenuating circumstances prevented the timely filing of
the request. Any supporting documentation must be submitted together with the request for
reconsideration. The Commission will consider requests for reconsideration filed after the
deadline only in very limited circumstances. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(c).

COMPLAINANT’S RIGHT TO FILE A CIVIL ACTION (R0610)
This is a decision requiring the Agency to continue its administrative processing of your complaint.
However, if you wish to file a civil action, you have the right to file such action in an appropriate
United States District Court within ninety (90) calendar days from the date that you receive this
decision. In the alternative, you may file a civil action after one hundred and eighty (180)
calendar days of the date you filed your complaint with the Agency, or filed your appeal with the
Commission. If you file a civil action, you must name as the defendant in the complaint the person
who is the official Agency head or department head, identifying that person by his or her full name
and official title. Failure to do so may result in the dismissal of your case in court. “Agency” or
“department” means the national organization, and not the local office, facility or department in
which you work. Filing a civil action will terminate the administrative processing of your
complaint.

 2019002184

8
RIGHT TO REQUEST COUNSEL (Z0815)
If you want to file a civil action but cannot pay the fees, costs, or security to do so, you may request
permission from the court to proceed with the civil action without paying these fees or costs.
Similarly, if you cannot afford an attorney to represent you in the civil action, you may request the
court to appoint an attorney for you. You must submit the requests for waiver of court costs or
appointment of an attorney directly to the court, not the Commission. The court has the sole
discretion to grant or deny these types of requests. Such requests do not alter the time limits for
filing a civil action (please read the paragraph titled Complainant’s Right to File a Civil Action for
the specific time limits).

The Agency further cites Otterstedt v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal No. 01A05235 (March 19,
2002) for the proposition that a complainant is deemed to have constructively received documents
mailed to his last known address when he fails to notify the agency of an address change, yet there
is no dispute regarding Complainant’s address in this matter. The Agency contends that an on-
point appeal is Mazurek v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Appeal Nos. 01A11033, 01995466 (January
23, 2002). We note, however, that in Mazurek , the Agency delivered the report of investigation
to the complainant’s post office box when certified -mail delivery failed , while delivery never
occurred in this instance.

We find the Agency’s argument that Complainant received constructive notice of his rights and
failed to act with due diligence unpersuasive. It is undisputed here that Complainant did not receive
a copy of the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing via certified mail or regular
mail prior to the issuance of the Agency’s final decision.

5
Moreover, Complainant immediately obtained legal counsel upon learning that procedural errors
existed, and Complainant’s counsel attempted to engage with the Agency regarding the errors .
The Agency has not demonstrated that Complainant was in actual receipt or had constructive
notice of the report of investigation and notice of the right to a hearing.

Further, to the extent the Agency asserts that Complainant filed an untimely hearin g request, we
note that the Commission has held that a complainant’s actual receipt of the notice of the right to
a hearing was necessary to commence the running of the time- limitation in which to request a
hearing. See Kellus v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC Request No. 05920198 (Apr. 20, 1992) (hearing
rights were sent certified mail and returned to the agency unclaimed and the agency failed to show
that the complainant actually received copies sent by regular mail) ; Battle v. U.S. Postal Serv.,
EEOC Request No. 05910441 (June 13, 1991) (complainant alleged that she did not receive a
proposed decision when certified mail was returned to the agency unclaimed, first -class mailing
was never returned, and the agency failed to provide evidence of proof of service).

Here, actual receipt of the investigative file did not occur until December 13, 2018, when the
Agency provided Complainant’s counsel with the investigative file. There is no evidence in the
record showing that Complainant received the report of investigation or notice of his right to a
hearing prior to this time , nor any indication in the record that the Agency made any additional
attempts to provide Complainant with the information after the certified mailing was returned. The
Agency provided an affidavit from the postal carrier who stated she left notice of the package.
However, Complainant stated that he received no such note. Contrary to the Agency’s assertion
that Complainant “at any time during the 30-calendar day period, could have requested redelivery
or designated someone to claim the report of investigation on his behalf,” the record does not
establish that Complainant had actual knowledge of the redelivery notice left at his door or the
contents of the undelivered package. Therefore, the Agency’s insinuation that Complainant sat on
his rights is purely speculative.

CONCLUSION

Accordingly, we find Complainant filed a timely hearing request when he requested a hearing on
December 19, 2018. Therefore, based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on
appeal, including those not specifically addressed herein, we VACATE the Agency’s final
decision and REMAND the entire complaint in accordance with the Order below.

the remanded complaint within fifteen (15) calendar days of the date this decision becomes final.

Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
February 26, 2019 final decision concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title

VACATES the Agency’s final decision and REMANDS t he matter to the Agency for further
processing.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Full- Time
Maintenance Mechanic, PS -07/O, at the Agency’s Chicago Metro Surface Hub in Elk Grove
Village, Illinois.

On July 7, 2019 (and later amended) , Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female), color (Black), and in reprisal for

career advancement;

4. On dates not specified, management did not correctly post EAS position vacancies;

5. On June 12, 2018, management reverted vacant maintenance positions; and

6. On July 17, 2018, Complainant was sent home, told not to return to work until she
had medical documentation for her recen t absence, and charged absence without
leave (AWOL) while she was off work at management’s instruction.

The Agency dismissed Claims (3) and (5) for failure to state a claim because these claims
constituted a collateral attack on a negotiated grievance settlement reached between the union and
Agency management under the collective bargaining agreement . The Agency also dismissed
Claim (4) for failure to state a claim because Complainant did not show that she was aggrieved by
this allegation.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency asserted that it provided Complainant with a
copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing before an
EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hea ring within the time
frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that management
subjected her to discrimination or reprisal as alleged.

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends that she never received the investigative report and was never
given an opportunity to request a hearing before an AJ. In addition, Complainant argues several
other procedural errors in the processing of her complaint. Accordingly, Complainant requests
that the Commission reverse the final decision.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f) provides in relevant part that the agency shall provide
the complainant with a copy of the investigative file and shall notify the complainant that, within
30 days of receipt of the investigative file, the complainant has the right to request a hearing and
decision from an Administrative Judge or may request an immediate final decision pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.110 from the agency with which the complaint was filed.

 2019003104

3
Complainant contends that the Agency did not provide her with the report of investigation and
notice of her right to request a hearing. The record contains a copy of the December 17, 2018
transmittal letter, the Request for Hearing form, and the report of investigation. The U.S. Postal
Service’s Priority Mail envelope for that letter contains a label dated January 17, 2019, stating that
the envelope was unclaimed and that the U.S. Postal Service was unable to forward the envelope.
The envelope was then returned to sender. T here is no evidence that Complainant received the
report of investigation or notice of her right to request a hearing.

The record therefore does not contain any evidence establishing that Complainant received the
report of investigation or was informed of her right to request a hearing. The Commission has
repeatedly stated that “the agency has the burden of providing evidence and/or proof to support its
final decisions.” Ericson v. Dep't of the Army, EEOC Request No. 05920623 (Jan. 14, 1993). As
such, the Commission finds that the Agency has not refuted Complainant’s contention that she did
not receive the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing. Thus, in the interest
of fundamental fairness and preservation of EEO rights, and because of the lack of persuasive
evidence establishing that Complainant received notice of her right to request a hearing, we fin d
that Complainant's complaint should be remanded for a hearing. See Maxima R. v. Dep’t of
Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 0120171171 (Nov. 9, 2018).

CONCLUSION

specifically addressed herein, we VACATE the Agency’s final decision and REMAND the matter
for further processing in accordance with the ORDER below.

DECISION

On March 30, 2019, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
February 26, 2019 final decision concerning her equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. For the following reasons, the Commission
VACATES the Agency’s final decision and REMANDS t he matter to the Agency for further
processing.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Full- Time
Maintenance Mechanic, PS -07/O, at the Agency’s Chicago Metro Surface Hub in Elk Grove
Village, Illinois.

On July 7, 2019 (and later amended) , Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against her on the bases of sex (female), color (Black), and in reprisal for
prior protected EEO activity when:

opportunities;

2. On or around February 13, 2018, Complainant was denied a detail opportunity and
career advancement;

3. On March 9, 2018, management reposted a previously eliminated position;

4. On dates not specified, management did not correctly post EAS position vacancies;

5. On June 12, 2018, management reverted vacant maintenance positions; and

6. On July 17, 2018, Complainant was sent home, told not to return to work until she
had medical documentation for her recen t absence, and charged absence without
leave (AWOL) while she was off work at management’s instruction.

The Agency dismissed Claims (3) and (5) for failure to state a claim because these claims
constituted a collateral attack on a negotiated grievance settlement reached between the union and
Agency management under the collective bargaining agreement . The Agency also dismissed
Claim (4) for failure to state a claim because Complainant did not show that she was aggrieved by
this allegation.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency asserted that it provided Complainant with a
copy of the report of investigation (ROI) and notice of her right to request a hearing before an
EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a hea ring within the time
frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that management
subjected her to discrimination or reprisal as alleged.

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant contends that she never received the investigative report and was never
given an opportunity to request a hearing before an AJ. In addition, Complainant argues several
other procedural errors in the processing of her complaint. Accordingly, Complainant requests
that the Commission reverse the final decision.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f) provides in relevant part that the agency shall provide
the complainant with a copy of the investigative file and shall notify the complainant that, within
30 days of receipt of the investigative file, the complainant has the right to request a hearing and
decision from an Administrative Judge or may request an immediate final decision pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.110 from the agency with which the complaint was filed.

 2019003104

3
Complainant contends that the Agency did not provide her with the report of investigation and
notice of her right to request a hearing. The record contains a copy of the December 17, 2018
transmittal letter, the Request for Hearing form, and the report of investigation. The U.S. Postal
Service’s Priority Mail envelope for that letter contains a label dated January 17, 2019, stating that
the envelope was unclaimed and that the U.S. Postal Service was unable to forward the envelope.
The envelope was then returned to sender. T here is no evidence that Complainant received the
report of investigation or notice of her right to request a hearing.

The record therefore does not contain any evidence establishing that Complainant received the
report of investigation or was informed of her right to request a hearing. The Commission has
repeatedly stated that “the agency has the burden of providing evidence and/or proof to support its
final decisions.” Ericson v. Dep't of the Army, EEOC Request No. 05920623 (Jan. 14, 1993). As
such, the Commission finds that the Agency has not refuted Complainant’s contention that she did
not receive the report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing. Thus, in the interest
of fundamental fairness and preservation of EEO rights, and because of the lack of persuasive
evidence establishing that Complainant received notice of her right to request a hearing, we fin d
that Complainant's complaint should be remanded for a hearing. See Maxima R. v. Dep’t of
Veterans Affairs, EEOC Appeal No. 0120171171 (Nov. 9, 2018).

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we VACATE the Agency’s final decision and REMAND the matter

The Agency shall take the following remedial action within thirty (30) days of the date this decision

The Agency shall issue to Complainant a copy of the investigative file, along with the

interviewed for the position. Id. at 35. Therefore, she was not selected for a vacant SBDO
position. According to Complainant, three individuals outside her protected classes were selected
for SBDO vacant positions under the job announcement.

On August 21, 2015, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency
discriminated against her on the bases of race (African -American), sex (female), and color
(brown) when on May 31, 2015, she discovered that she was not selected for the position of
Supervisory Behavioral Detection Officer (SBDO), Job Opportunity Announcement N o. LAX-
15-894637.

Following the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the report of
investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing but
subsequently withdrew her request. Consequently, the Agency issued a final decision pursuant to
29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b). The decision concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the
Agency subjected her to discrimination as alleged.

The Agency found that it articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for Complainant’s
non-selection, which Complainant did no show were pretextual. In so finding, the A gency
referred to a Human Resources (HR) Representative who noted that "a current employee's
[resume] must show that they have the experience, backed -up by their SF50s showing their
position or SF52s (or detail document) showing that they have the experience." The Agency
noted that Complainant conceded that her official personnel file did not incl ude an SF-50 or SF-
52 demonstrating the req uired experience for the SBDO position. The Agency noted that
Complainant’s resume did not demonstrate six months of experience as a work leader, team
leader, or supervisor in the private sector in accordance with the Job Opportunity
Announcement. The Agency also observed that Complainant stated that she did not know who
the responsible management official was and if he/she knew of her protected clas ses. The
Agency therefore found that Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to
discrimination.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), the Agency's decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.405(a). See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part
1614, at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review
“requires that the Commission examine the record without regard to the factual and legal
determinations of the previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents,
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and r elevant submissions of the
parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and
its interpretation of the law”).

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Non-Selection
To prevail in a disparate treatment claim, a complainant mus t satisfy the three -part evidentiary
scheme fashioned by the Supreme Court in McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792
(1973). A complainant must initially establish a prima facie case by demonstrating that he was
subjected to an adverse employment action under circumstances that would support an inference
of discrimination. Furnco Constr. Co. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567, 576 (1978). Proof of a prima
facie case will vary depending on the facts of the particular case. McDonnell Douglas , 441 U.S.
at 802 n. 13. The burden then shifts to the agency to articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory
reason for its actions. Texas Dep't of Cmty. Affairs v. Burdine , 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). To
ultimately prevail, a complainant must prove, by a preponderance of the evidence, that the
agency's explanation is a pretext for discrimination. Reeves v. Sanderson Plumbing Products,
Inc., 530 U.S. 133, 143 (2000); St. Mary's Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502, 519 (1993).
Upon review, we find that assuming, arguendo , Complainant established a prima facie case of
discrimination based her protected classes, the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory
reasons for Complainant's non-selection. We note that a HR Representative noted via email that
Complainant’s resume did not demonstrate six months of experience as a work leader, team
leader, or supervisor in the private sector in accordance with the Job Opportunity
Announcement. ROI, at 71- 73. The HR Representative noted that Complainant ’s official
personnel file did not include the proper documentation showing the requisite experience for the
SBDO position. Id.
The burden now shifts to Complainant to establish that the Agency's nondiscriminatory reasons
were pretext for discrimination. Burdine , at 256. In an attempt to show pretext, Complainant
averred that three individuals outside her protected classes with less experience than her were
selected under the Job Opportunity Announcement.
Upon review, we find that Complainant has not established that the Agency’s reasons for her
non-selection were pretextual based on her protected classes. In so finding, we note that on May
29, 2015, a HR Representative documented that Complainant’s resume did not “ demonstrate
experience as a work leader, team leader, or supervisor in the private sector to meet the 6 months
requirement.” ROI. at 73. Even assuming, that this HR Representative made a mistake in finding
that Complainant did not meet the job qualifications under the announcement , Complainant has
not shown that any such mistake was motivated by discriminatory animus.
CONCLUSION

We AFFRIM the Agency’s final decision finding no discrimination.

The Commission's regulations allow an AJ to grant summary judgment when he or she finds that
there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). An issue of fact is “genuine”
if the evidence is such that a reasonable fact finder could find in favor of the non- moving party.
Celotex v. Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322-23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105
(1st Cir. 1988). A fact is “material” if it has the potential to affect the outcome of the case. In
rendering this appellate decision we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and factual conclusions, and
the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo . See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a)(stating that a
“decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on a de novo review…”); see

110), at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (as revised, August 5, 2015)(providing that an administrative j udge’s
determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed
de novo).

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s July 2, 2019, final order
concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging employment
discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as
amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the following reasons, the Commission AFFIRMS the
Agency’s final order.

ISSUE PRESENTED

The issue is whether the Administrative Judge properly dismissed Complainant’s class complaint.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail H andler at the
Agency’s Dallas Network Distribution Center in Dallas, Texas. On June 16, 2017, the Agency
issued Notices of Abolishment of Position to Complainant and other Mail Handlers.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2019004890

2
They were informed that they would be “unassigned regular” full-time employees, effective June
24, 2017, and were encouraged to bid on posted duty-assignments. On June 28, 2017, the Agency
rescinded all the notices of abolishment and the employees were instructed to report for their
regular schedules on July 8, 2017.

On June 28, 2017, Complainant initiated pre-complaint counseling alleging age discrimination in
a class action complaint. On July 10, 2017, the Agency sent Complainant information on the
processing of class complaints. T he Agency informed Complainant that class complaints were
processed differently than individual complaints of discrimination; f or example, that a class
complaint is not investigated by the Agency but is forwarded to the nearest EEOC office where an
Administrative Judge (AJ) is appointed to make an initial determination to accept or dismiss the
complaint.

On September 22, 2017, the Agency issued Complainant his notice of right to file a formal
complaint. On September 25, 2017, Complainant filed a formal class complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against the class members on the basis of age when on June 16, 2017, Senior
Mail Handlers received letters abolishing their bid assignments. On October 16, 2017, the Agency
forwarded the class complaint to the EEOC’s Dallas District Office.

On May 10, 2019, the AJ issued an Order to Show Cause to determine if a liv e claim remained
following the resolution during the grievance process, which resulted in the Agency rescinding the
letters. Complainant timely responded to the AJ’s order and stated that the Agency did not
completely restore his abolished position. Specifically, Complainant stated that his off days were
changed to Fridays and Saturdays, and that the Agency refused to change them to Saturdays and
Sundays.

On June 7, 2019, the AJ issued an Order Entering Dismissal pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.107(a)(5), finding that the complaint was moot. The AJ found that the record showed that
the Agency rescinded the letters of job abolishment, which placed the affected Mail Handlers back
into their jobs with appropriate backpay. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting
the AJ’s dismissal , and it also concluded that Complainant’s individual complaint of
discrimination was subject to dismissal as moot for the same reasons that support the dismissal of
the class complaint.
2

Complainant filed the instant appeal and submitted a statement in support of his appeal. The
Agency opposed Complainant’s appeal.

2 We note that the Commission has the discretion to review only those issues specifically raised in
an appeal. See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614,
at Chap. 9, § IV.A.3 (Aug. 5, 2015). On appeal, Complainant did not contest the Agency’s
dismissal of his individual claim of discrimination; as such, we will not address th at claim in the
instant decision.

 2019004890

3
CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant argues that the Agency failed to notify all the class members that the class
action was accepted or provide Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation, which led
to the denial of an opportunity to request a hearing.

The Agency counters that Complainant’s appeal rests on his incorrect interpretation of the
Commission’s complaint processing regulations. The Agency notes that the class complaint was
not “accepted,” and it followed the Commission’s regulations to issue a final order following the
AJ’s decision. The Agency states that because this was a class complaint, it was referred directly
to the Commission, and no investigation was undertaken. The Agency also asserts that
Complainant’s claim that the Agency and AJ had access to information that he did not have is
untrue because he was issued a copy of the Counselor’s Report at the same time that it was referred
to the EEOC’s Dallas District Office.

The Agency states that the AJ determined that no hearing was necessary because there was no
controversy remaining and no remedy available to the class, and that Complainant did not provide
information about what evidence he and the class was prepared to offer at a hearing. The Agency
requests that the Commission affirm its final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal of Complainant’s
class complaint.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.204(d) provides that within 30 days of an agency’s receipt of
a class complaint, the agency shall designate an agency representative and forward the complaint
to the Commission. Initially, the AJ may dismiss the complaint on procedural bases found at 29
C.F.R. § 1614.107, or because the complaint does not meet the prerequisites for certifying a class
complaint under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.204(a)(2); see also Equal Employment Opportunity
Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD -110), at Chap. 8 § IV (Aug. 5, 2015)
(Administrative Judge shall issue a decision on whether to certify or dismiss a class complaint).

In this case, Complainant argues that the Agency failed to provide him with a copy of the report
of investigation, which led to the denial of an opportunity to request a hearing. However, we find
that the Agency properly processed Complainant’s class complaint. In accordance with 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614. 204(d), the Agency timely forwarded the class complaint to the Commission within 30
days of receipt of the formal class complaint; as such, the Agency did not produce a report of
investigation. To the extent that Complainant argues that he was denied the documents provided
to the AJ, we note that Complainant was carbon copied on the Agency’s submission to the EEOC
Dallas District Office.

Complainant also argues that the Agency failed to notify the class members that the class action
was accepted. However, the record shows that the class action complaint was dismissed, and not
accepted by the AJ.

 2019004890

4
It is undisputed that on June 28, 2017, the Agency rescinded all the letters informing the Mail
Handlers that their assignments were abolished. EEOC regulation provides that a complaint shall
be dismissed if the matter is moot in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107( a)(5). As such, we find that the AJ
properly dismissed Complainant’s class complaint for being moot.

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal
of Complainant’s class complaint.

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s July 2, 2019, final order

discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as
amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. For the following reasons, the Commission AFFIRMS the
Agency’s final order.

The issue is whether the Administrative Judge properly dismissed Complainant’s class complaint.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Mail H andler at the
Agency’s Dallas Network Distribution Center in Dallas, Texas. On June 16, 2017, the Agency
issued Notices of Abolishment of Position to Complainant and other Mail Handlers.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2019004890

They were informed that they would be “unassigned regular” full-time employees, effective June
24, 2017, and were encouraged to bid on posted duty-assignments. On June 28, 2017, the Agency
rescinded all the notices of abolishment and the employees were instructed to report for their
regular schedules on July 8, 2017.

On June 28, 2017, Complainant initiated pre-complaint counseling alleging age discrimination in
a class action complaint. On July 10, 2017, the Agency sent Complainant information on the
processing of class complaints. T he Agency informed Complainant that class complaints were
processed differently than individual complaints of discrimination; f or example, that a class
complaint is not investigated by the Agency but is forwarded to the nearest EEOC office where an
Administrative Judge (AJ) is appointed to make an initial determination to accept or dismiss the
complaint.

On September 22, 2017, the Agency issued Complainant his notice of right to file a formal
complaint. On September 25, 2017, Complainant filed a formal class complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against the class members on the basis of age when on June 16, 2017, Senior
Mail Handlers received letters abolishing their bid assignments. On October 16, 2017, the Agency
forwarded the class complaint to the EEOC’s Dallas District Office.

On May 10, 2019, the AJ issued an Order to Show Cause to determine if a liv e claim remained
following the resolution during the grievance process, which resulted in the Agency rescinding the
letters. Complainant timely responded to the AJ’s order and stated that the Agency did not
completely restore his abolished position. Specifically, Complainant stated that his off days were
changed to Fridays and Saturdays, and that the Agency refused to change them to Saturdays and
Sundays.

On June 7, 2019, the AJ issued an Order Entering Dismissal pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.107(a)(5), finding that the complaint was moot. The AJ found that the record showed that
the Agency rescinded the letters of job abolishment, which placed the affected Mail Handlers back
into their jobs with appropriate backpay. The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting
the AJ’s dismissal , and it also concluded that Complainant’s individual complaint of
discrimination was subject to dismissal as moot for the same reasons that support the dismissal of
the class complaint.
2

Complainant filed the instant appeal and submitted a statement in support of his appeal. The
Agency opposed Complainant’s appeal.

2 We note that the Commission has the discretion to review only those issues specifically raised in
an appeal. See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614,

dismissal of his individual claim of discrimination; as such, we will not address th at claim in the
instant decision.

 2019004890

3
CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

On appeal, Complainant argues that the Agency failed to notify all the class members that the class
action was accepted or provide Complainant with a copy of the report of investigation, which led
to the denial of an opportunity to request a hearing.

The Agency counters that Complainant’s appeal rests on his incorrect interpretation of the
Commission’s complaint processing regulations. The Agency notes that the class complaint was
not “accepted,” and it followed the Commission’s regulations to issue a final order following the
AJ’s decision. The Agency states that because this was a class complaint, it was referred directly
to the Commission, and no investigation was undertaken. The Agency also asserts that
Complainant’s claim that the Agency and AJ had access to information that he did not have is
untrue because he was issued a copy of the Counselor’s Report at the same time that it was referred
to the EEOC’s Dallas District Office.

The Agency states that the AJ determined that no hearing was necessary because there was no
controversy remaining and no remedy available to the class, and that Complainant did not provide
information about what evidence he and the class was prepared to offer at a hearing. The Agency
requests that the Commission affirm its final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal of Complainant’s
class complaint.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.204(d) provides that within 30 days of an agency’s receipt of
a class complaint, the agency shall designate an agency representative and forward the complaint
to the Commission. Initially, the AJ may dismiss the complaint on procedural bases found at 29
C.F.R. § 1614.107, or because the complaint does not meet the prerequisites for certifying a class
complaint under 29 C.F.R. § 1614.204(a)(2); see also Equal Employment Opportunity
Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD -110), at Chap. 8 § IV (Aug. 5, 2015)
(Administrative Judge shall issue a decision on whether to certify or dismiss a class complaint).

In this case, Complainant argues that the Agency failed to provide him with a copy of the report
of investigation, which led to the denial of an opportunity to request a hearing. However, we find
that the Agency properly processed Complainant’s class complaint. In accordance with 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614. 204(d), the Agency timely forwarded the class complaint to the Commission within 30
days of receipt of the formal class complaint; as such, the Agency did not produce a report of
investigation. To the extent that Complainant argues that he was denied the documents provided
to the AJ, we note that Complainant was carbon copied on the Agency’s submission to the EEOC
Dallas District Office.

Complainant also argues that the Agency failed to notify the class members that the class action
was accepted. However, the record shows that the class action complaint was dismissed, and not
accepted by the AJ.

 2019004890

4

be dismissed if the matter is moot in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107( a)(5). As such, we find that the AJ
properly dismissed Complainant’s class complaint for being moot.

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal
of Complainant’s class complaint.

selection process. [F1] conduc ted a general review of all th e resumes and identified the top
competitive resumes. His first pass review reduced the pool by about half. Complainant did not

subjected to discrimination. The AJ found th at Complainant failed to submit medical
documentation that she wanted to be considered for Schedule A hiring in a timely manner. AJ
Decision at 7. The AJ further found that Compla inant failed to establish that the Agency’s
articulated reasons for its actions were pretext for discrimination.
The Agency subsequently issued a final order on August 6, 2019 adopting the AJ’s finding of no
discrimination.
2
The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant submitted a statement that was not
responsive to the AJ’s decision or the Agency’s final action.
In response, the Agency’s requests that we affirm its final action.
2 We presume, for purposes of analysis only and without so finding, that Complainant is an
individual with a disability.

3 2019005653
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS
In rendering this appellate decision we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and factual conclusions, and
the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo . See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a) (stating that a
“decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on a de novo review . . .”);
see also Equal Employment Opportunity Manageme nt Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO
MD-110), at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (Aug. 5, 2015) (p roviding that an administrative judge’s
determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed
de novo). This essentially means that we should look at this case with fresh eyes. In other words,
we are free to accept (if accurate) or reject (if erroneous) the AJ’s, and Agency’s, factual
conclusions and legal analysis – including on the ultimate fact of whether intentional
discrimination occurred, and on the legal issue of whether any federal employment discrimination
statute was violated. See id. at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (explaining that the de novo standard of review
“requires that the Commission examine the record without regard to the factual and legal
determinations of the previous decision ma ker,” and that EEOC “review the documents,
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and relevant submissions of the parties,
and . . . issue its decision based on the Commi ssion’s own assessment of the record and its
interpretation of the law”).
The Commission’s regulations allow an AJ to issue a decision without a hearing upon finding that
there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). EEOC’s decision without a
hearing regulation follows the summary judgment procedure from federal court. Fed. R. Civ. P.
56. The U.S. Supreme Court held summary judgment is appropriate where a judge determines no
genuine issue of material fact exists under the legal and evidentiary standards. Anderson v. Liberty
Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 255 (1986). In ruling on a summary judgment motion, the judge is to
determine whether there are genuine issues for tr ial, as opposed to weighing the evidence. Id. at
249. At the summary judgment stage, the judge must believe the non-moving party’s evidence and
must draw justifiable inferences in the non-moving party’s favor. Id. at 255. A “genuine issue of
fact” is one that a reasonable judge could find in favor for the non-moving party. Celotex v. Catrett,
477 U.S. 317, 322-23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir. 1988). A
“material” fact has the potential to affect the outcome of a case.
To successfully oppose a decision by summary judgment, a complainant must identify, with
specificity, facts in dispute eith er within the record or by producing further supporting evidence
and must further establish that such facts are ma terial under applicable law. Here, Complainant
has failed to point with adequate specificity to particular evidence in the investigative file or other
evidence of record that indicates such a dispute. For the reasons discussed below, we find that,
even construing any inferences raised by th e undisputed facts in favor of Complainant, a
reasonable fact-finder could not find in her favor.
A claim of disparate treatment is examined unde r the three-part analysis first enunciated in
McDonnell Douglas Corp. v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973) . For complainant to prevail, she must
first establish a prima facie case of discrimination by presenting facts that, if unexplained,
reasonably give rise to an infe rence of discrimination, i.e., that a prohibited consideration was a

4 2019005653
factor in the adverse employment action. Se e McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco
Construction Corp. v. Waters, 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the agency to
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. See Texas Dep’t of Cmty. Affairs
v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the agency has met its burden, the complainant bears
the ultimate responsibility to persuade the fact finder by a preponderance of the evidence that the
agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S.
502 (1993).
This established order of analysis in discrimination cases, in which the first step normally consists
of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases. Where the
agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action at issue, the
factual inquiry can proceed directly to the thir d step of the McDonnell Douglas analysis, the
ultimate issue of whether complainant has show n by a preponderance of the evidence that the
agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Serv. Bd. of Governors v.
Aikens, 460 U.S. 711, 713-714 (1983); Hernandez v. Dep’t of Transportation, EEOC Request No.
05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Dep’t of Health and Human Services, EEOC Request No.
05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. Dep’t of the Navy, EEOC Petition No. 03900056 (May
31, 1990).
The Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. The record contains
two declarations under penalty of perjury from F1. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 163, F1’s
Declaration Under Penalty of Perjury June 6, 2019 (F1’s Dec). F1 asserts that human resources
sent him all resumes that met minimum qualifications. ROI at 164. F1 states that he conducted a
general review of all the resumes he received from human resources and reduced the applicant
pool by half based on this initial review. Id. Complainant’s application did not progress beyond
the initial screening by F1. Id. at 170. F1 asse rts that he selected the top candidates for further
review and interviews, and Complainant was not selected to continue on in the process. F1 stated
that Complainant was considered to be less competitive in terms of experience and qualifications.
ROI at 170. F1 stated that they received 440 applications for the position in question. F1’s Dec.
F1 noted that while he did not independently recollect Complainant’s application, Complainant’s
resume indicated that she had a gap in her employment. F1’s Dec.
Regarding the Schedule A hiring, the record co ntains a declaration of perjury from a Human
Resources Specialist (HR1). ROI at 234. Ther ein, HR1 states that she received an email from
Complainant indicating that she is disabled and requesting placement on a non-competitive hiring
process. Id. at 237. HR1 asserts that she responded to the email informing Complainant that she
did not indicate on her application that she wanted to be considered as a Schedule A applicant and
that she did not include Schedule A documentation. Id. HR1 further asserts that she subsequently
provided Complainant with a sample Schedule A letter. Id. HR1 asserts that Complainant did not
submit a Schedule A letter during this time.
3 Id. at 238.
3 The record reflects that the Agency notified Complainant on November 16, 2017 that the hiring
process had been completed and she was not selected. ROI at 363.

5 2019005653
Complainant failed to establish that the Agency’s articulated reason was pretext for discrimination.
The record contains a copy of the job announcement for the position in question. The duties of
the position include litigating “a broad range of ca ses involving significant, complex issues on
behalf of the United States in federal court…working in the Criminal Division.” Report of
Investigation (ROI) at 344. The records supports the AJ’s determination that:
“no reasonable factfinder, even viewing the light most favorable to Complainant,
could conclude her qualifications were plainly superior to the eventual
selectees….Though Complainant met the bare minimum qualifications for
consideration for this position, she was objectively less qualified than the selectees.
Although this was a prosecutor position, Complainant had no criminal law
experience. Rather, as indicated in her resume, her litigation experience was
limited to civil cases…Moreover, she ha d no public sector or public service
experience. By comparison, the individuals granted interviews came with strong
backgrounds in criminal prosecution or bi g law complex civil litigation, and/or
federal clerkships.” AJ Decision at 6.

hearing finding no discrimination.

stated in the Agency’s final decision. Our review of the record reflects that Complainant
checked “age” as the only basis raised in box 14 on his formal complaint. We further note that
on April 1, 2019, the Agency issued a Notice of Acceptance informing Complainant that the
accepted claim for investigation only included age as a raised basis. The record r eflects that
Complainant did not dispute the Agency’s determination for his accepted claim even though the
Notice of Acceptance provided Complainant the opportunity to do so within seven days of
receipt of the notice. Moreover, the report of investigation indicates that Complainant did not
complete or submit an affidavit to the EEO investigator. Therefore, Complainant may not, for the
first time on appeal, dispute the basis raised. Thus, we find that age is the only raised basis in the
instant complaint.

of the evidence that the agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor
Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

consists of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases.

2019005983

3
Where the agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action
at issue, the factual inquiry can proceed directly to the third step of the McDonnell Douglas
analysis, the ultimate issue of whether complainant has shown by a preponderance of the
evidence that the agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Service
Board of Governors v. Aikens , 460 U.S. 711, 713- 714 (1983); Hernandez v. Depar tment of
Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Department of Health
and Human Services, EEOC Request No. 05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. Department
of the Navy, EEOC Petition No. 03900056 (May 31, 1990).

The Agency provided legitimate, non- discriminatory reasons for not providing Complainant
overtime. Complainant’s first level supervisor (“S1”) testified that he stopped Complainant’s
overtime in December 2018, because there were not enough work hours available for
Complainant to complete without violat ing Complainant’s medical restrictions. S1 explained
that Complainant’s work restrictions prevented him from lifting, pushing, or pulling more than
15 pounds , driving any type of equipment, making repetitive motions with his hands - like
writing, or reaching above his shoulders. S1 stated that Complainant was authorized overtime
for all boiler room responsibilities . However, because of Complainant’s work restrictions,
Complainant could only monitor the boilers, chill ers, air compressors, and air d ryers. S1
clarified that all filter replacements and repairs had to be completed by other staff. However, S1
explained that the boilers and chillers were removed from the facility on November 8, 2018.

S1 further explained that he declined Complainant’s suggestion to move some of Complainant’s
regularly scheduled work assignments (monitoring the boilers, chillers, air compressors, and air
dryers) to the weekend so that Complainant could work overtime hours on Saturdays. S1
reasoned that with the boilers and chillers removed, only 3 -4 hours were needed to complete
tasks associated with the air compressors and air dryers and S1 already had four regularly
scheduled Saturday employees to complete these tasks. S1 acknowledged that he allowed
Complainant to work overtime on December 12, 2018, to service the air compressor and air
driers for three hours, but Complainant spent his remaining overtime hours “w andering around
the facility.”

After careful consideration of the record, we con clude that neither during the investigation, nor
on appeal, has Complainant proven, by a preponderance of the evidence, that these proffere d
reasons for the disputed actions were a pretext for unlawful discrimination based on
Complainant’s age.

We AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision because the preponderance of the evidence of record
does not establish that discrimination occurred.

DECISION

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) accepts
Complainant’s appeal, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s August 6, 2019
final decision concerning an equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint claiming
employment discrimination in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act of 1967
(ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq.

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Building Equipment Mechanic at the
Agency’s Atlanta Processing and Distribution Center in Atlanta, Georgia.

On March 20, 2019, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint claiming that the Agency
discriminated against him based on age ( YOB: 1939) when, since December 1, 2018,
Complainant has not been provided with overtime.

After the investigation of th e accepted claims, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of
the report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before a n EEOC

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2019005983

2
Administrative Judge (AJ) or a final decision within thirty days of receipt of the correspondence.
Complainant did not respond.

On August 6, 2019, the Agency issued the instant final decision, pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination.

The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant argues that the Agency analyzed the
wrong basis. Specifically, Complainant argues that he raised disability, not age, as a basis in his
formal complaint.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Preliminary Matter – Basis Raised

As an initial matter, we address Complainant’s argument that he raised disability, not his age, as
stated in the Agency’s final decision. Our review of the record reflects that Complainant
checked “age” as the only basis raised in box 14 on his formal complaint. We further note that
on April 1, 2019, the Agency issued a Notice of Acceptance informing Complainant that the
accepted claim for investigation only included age as a raised basis. The record r eflects that
Complainant did not dispute the Agency’s determination for his accepted claim even though the
Notice of Acceptance provided Complainant the opportunity to do so within seven days of
receipt of the notice. Moreover, the report of investigation indicates that Complainant did not
complete or submit an affidavit to the EEO investigator. Therefore, Complainant may not, for the
first time on appeal, dispute the basis raised. Thus, we find that age is the only raised basis in the
instant complaint.

Disparate Treatment

A claim of disparate treatment is examined under the three -part analysis first enunciated in
McDonnell Douglas Corporation v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For complainant to prevail, she
must first establish a prima facie of discrimination by presenting facts that, if unexplained,
reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e. , that a prohibited consideration was a
factor in the adverse employment action. See McDonnell Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco
Construction Corp. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The burden then shifts to the agency to
articulate a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for its actions. See Texas Department of
Community Affairs v. Burdine, 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the agency has met its burden,
the complainant bears the ultimate responsibility to persuade the fact finder by a preponderance
of the evidence that the agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. See St. Mary’s Honor
Center v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

This established order of analysis in discrimination cases, in which the first step normally
consists of determining the existence of a prima facie case, need not be followed in all cases.

2019005983

3
Where the agency has articulated a legitimate, nondiscriminatory reason for the personnel action
at issue, the factual inquiry can proceed directly to the third step of the McDonnell Douglas
analysis, the ultimate issue of whether complainant has shown by a preponderance of the
evidence that the agency’s actions were motivated by discrimination. See U.S. Postal Service
Board of Governors v. Aikens , 460 U.S. 711, 713- 714 (1983); Hernandez v. Depar tment of
Transportation, EEOC Request No. 05900159 (June 28, 1990); Peterson v. Department of Health
and Human Services, EEOC Request No. 05900467 (June 8, 1990); Washington v. Department
of the Navy, EEOC Petition No. 03900056 (May 31, 1990).

The Agency provided legitimate, non- discriminatory reasons for not providing Complainant
overtime. Complainant’s first level supervisor (“S1”) testified that he stopped Complainant’s
overtime in December 2018, because there were not enough work hours available for
Complainant to complete without violat ing Complainant’s medical restrictions. S1 explained
that Complainant’s work restrictions prevented him from lifting, pushing, or pulling more than
15 pounds , driving any type of equipment, making repetitive motions with his hands - like
writing, or reaching above his shoulders. S1 stated that Complainant was authorized overtime
for all boiler room responsibilities . However, because of Complainant’s work restrictions,
Complainant could only monitor the boilers, chill ers, air compressors, and air d ryers. S1
clarified that all filter replacements and repairs had to be completed by other staff. However, S1
explained that the boilers and chillers were removed from the facility on November 8, 2018.

S1 further explained that he declined Complainant’s suggestion to move some of Complainant’s
regularly scheduled work assignments (monitoring the boilers, chillers, air compressors, and air
dryers) to the weekend so that Complainant could work overtime hours on Saturdays. S1
reasoned that with the boilers and chillers removed, only 3 -4 hours were needed to complete
tasks associated with the air compressors and air dryers and S1 already had four regularly
scheduled Saturday employees to complete these tasks. S1 acknowledged that he allowed
Complainant to work overtime on December 12, 2018, to service the air compressor and air
driers for three hours, but Complainant spent his remaining overtime hours “w andering around
the facility.”

After careful consideration of the record, we con clude that neither during the investigation, nor
on appeal, has Complainant proven, by a preponderance of the evidence, that these proffere d
reasons for the disputed actions were a pretext for unlawful discrimination based on
Complainant’s age.

We AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision because the preponderance of the evidence of record
does not establish that discrimination occurred.
