The Agency accepted claim (1) for investigation. However, the Agency dismissed claim (2) on
procedural grounds. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 40-41. In a September 19, 2019 Order on
Initial Conference, the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) noted that Complainant does not contest
the dismissed claim. In addition, Complainant does not expressly contest the dismissed claim on
appeal. Thus, we decline to address the dismissed claim further herein.
Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ.
On October 23, 2019, the EEOC AJ issued a decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on
procedural grounds. To the extent that Complainan t was alleging that he was subjected to
discrimination based on the Agency’s April 17, 2018 mid-term progress review, the AJ dismissed
this matter for failure to state a claim and for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action. The
AJ further found that the crux of Complainant’s claim were the comments in his 2017 (rather than
2018) performance evaluation. To the extent Co mplainant was challenging his 2017 evaluation,
the EEOC AJ dismissed this claim for untimely EEO Counselor contact. The AJ reasoned that
Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation was dated October 17, 2017, for its final rating but
Complainant did not initiate EEO Counselor contact until May 4, 2018, outside of the applicable
time period.
On November 26, 2019, the Agency issued a final order implementing the AJ’s decision
dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds.
Complainant does not submit a statement or brief on appeal.
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS
We find that to the extent Complainant alle ged discrimination based on his 2018 mid-year
evaluation, the Agency properly dismissed this matter for alleging a proposal to take a personnel
action. EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107 (a)(5) p rovides that an agency shall dismiss a
complaint that alleges that a proposal to take a personnel action, or other preliminary step to taking
a personnel action, is discriminatory. The Commissi on has held that a periodic progress review
does not create a personal harm. See Jackson v. Central Intelligence Agency, EEOC Request No.
05931177 (June 24, 1994).
In the instant matter, the EEO Counselor’s Repo rt lists April 2018 as the date of the alleged
discriminatory incident. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 17-18. The record reflects that a progress
review was issued to Complainant on April 17, 2018 and that Complainant refused to sign it. ROI
at 116. Because this claim involved an alleged di scriminatory progress review, we find that the
Agency properly dismissed this matter for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action.

20200018413
We concur with the AJ that the crux of Co mplainant’s claim is his 2017 (rather than 2018)
performance evaluation. The record contains a declaration under penalty from Complainant. ROI
at 56. Therein, Complainant expressly sets forth the negative comments that he received in an
evaluation which he alleges encompasses his claim. ROI at 58. The record reflects that these
comments were made in Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation. ROI at 117. Complainant
also lists in his declaration under penalty a named management official (Q1) who he alleges is the
responsible management official. ROI at 58. The record reflects that Q1 was the rating official in
Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation and not his 2018 evaluation. ROI at 117, 64.
EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.105(a)(1) requires that complaints of discrimination should
be brought to the attention of the Equal Employment Opportunity Counselor within forty-five (45)
days of the date of the matter al leged to be discriminatory or, in the case of a personnel action,
within forty-five (45) days of the effective date of the action. The Commission has adopted a
"reasonable suspicion" standard (as opposed to a "supportive facts" standard) to determine when
the forty-five (45) day limitation period is triggered. See Howard v. Dep’t of the Navy, EEOC
Request No. 05970852 (Feb. 11, 1999). Thus, th e time limitation is not triggered until a
complainant reasonably suspects discrimination, but before all the facts that support a charge of
discrimination have become apparent.
EEOC Regulations provide that the agency or the Commission shall extend the time limits when
the individual shows that he was not notified of the time limits and was not otherwise aware of
them, that he did not know and reasonably should not have known that the discriminatory matter
or personnel action occurred, that despite due diligence he was prevented by circumstances beyond
his control from contacting the Counselor within the time limits, or for other reasons considered
sufficient by the agency or the Commission.
We find that the AJ properly dismissed Comp lainant’s claim regarding his 2017 performance
evaluation for untimely EEO Counsel or contact. The record contains a copy of Complainant’s
2017 performance evaluation reflecting that he received progress reviews on March 14, 2017, and
July 7, 2017, and a final evaluation on October 1 7, 2017. ROI at 117. The record reflects that
Complainant initiated EEO contact on May 4, 2018, more than 45 days from when he received his
final rating for his 2017 performance evaluatio n. Complainant does no t provide sufficient
justification for extending the applicable time limit.
Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final action implementing the EEOC AJ’s decision
dismissing Complainant’s complaint.

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as an Attorney Advisor in Norfolk,
Virginia. On September 16, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency
subjected her to discrimination based on race (African-American).

In its final decision, dated January 8, 2020, the Agency determined that Complainant’s complaint
was comprised of the following claim:

The Agency dismissed the formal complaint on the grounds tha t Complainant previously raised
the same claim which is currently pending before the EEOC. The Agency reasoned that
Complainant previously raised this matter in a prior EEO complaint, Agency Case No. HS-USCG-
00420-2018 and is pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Specifically, the Agency
stated “[t]he record showed Complainant not only recited identical facts, but also implicated
identical responsible management officials with very slight exceptions.” Final Agency Decision
at 2.

The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant asserts that the Agency’s framing of her
claim does not fully capture all her issues. Specifically, Complainant states that “the elements of
the current complaint are not identical …[to] the matter pending before t he EEOC because the
[prior] complaint does not allege that the Agency used a fraudulent position description…as a basis
of discrimination…The use of the fraudulent position description as alleged in the signed statement
of [C1] was not investigated as part of [the prior complaint]…” Complainant also asserts that she
has named several individuals as responsible management officials that she did not name in the
prior complaint.

In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision dismissing Complainant’s
complaint. The Agency further asserts that the fact that C1 was unhappy with her assigned duties
is immaterial to either of her complaints.

The regulation set forth at 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1) provides that the agency shall dismiss a
complaint that states the same claim that is pending before or has been decided by the agency or
Commission.

The Agency properly dismissed Complainant’s compla int for previously raising the same matter
which is currently pending before the Commission. Commission records reflect that Agency Case
No. HS-USCG-00420-2018 is currently pending before an EEOC AJ , EEOC Hearing No. 430-

claims in her prior complaint. Specifically, the Agency accepted the following claim:

greater volume of work than the current female incumbent who was hired at the

Attorney Advisor…[C1] explained that she is only responsible for civilian
personnel matters and that the position description was fraudulent because
according to the position description and the job announcement she was a general
law attorney required to handle real property, environmental law, ethics etc.

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission) from the Agency's decision dated February 13, 2020, dismissing his complaint of
unlawful employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was a former Police Officer, GS-
7, at the Agency’s West Roxbury VA Medical Center (VAMC) facility in West Roxbury,
Massachusetts.

On March 15, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected him
to unlawful retaliation for prior protected EEO activity when, on February 7, 2019, he was placed
on a cautionary list of employees who left the Agency under negative terms, including conduct
unbecoming.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2020002938

2
The Agency accepted the complaint and conducted an investigation which revealed the following
pertinent results.

Complainant was employed at the Agency from January 19, 2010 to February 3, 2013.

In March 2015, Complainant’s name was added to a “Cautionary List,” which was a list of former
employees known only to the Human Resources Division of the VA Boston Healthcare System
and prospective Agency employers.

On or about November 1, 2018, Complainant received a report of investigation for an unrelated
complaint indicating that he had been placed on the “Cautionary List” for former employees.

On December 15, 2018, Complainant submitted a request under the Freedom of Information Act
for a copy of the “Cautionary List that the VA Boston Healthcare Human Resources
Employee/Labor Relations keeps on file [which] documents former employees who left the facility
under negative terms including conduct unbecoming.”

On February 7, 2019, the Agency responded to Complainant’s request and provided a document
indicating Complainant’s name was on the Cautionary List.

On February 11, 2019, Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor regarding the instant complaint.

After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely
requested a hearing. The Agency submitted a Motion to D ismiss. The AJ subsequently issued a
Decision and Order dismissing the complaint pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2), for untimely
EEO Counselor contact.

The Agency issued its final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal. The instant appeal followed.
 ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.105(a)(1) requires that complaints of discrimination be
brought to the attention of the Equal Employment Opportunity Counselor within forty-five (45)
days of the date of the matter alleged to be discriminatory or, in the case of a personnel action,
within forty-five (45) days of the effective date of the action. The Commission has adopted a
“reasonable suspicion” standard (as opposed to a “supportive facts” standard) to determine when
the forty-five (45) day limitation period is triggered. See Howard v. Dep't of the Navy, EEOC
Request No. 05970852 (Feb. 11, 1999). Thus, the time limitation is not triggered until a
complainant reasonably suspects discrimination, but before all the facts that support a charge of
discrimination have become apparent.

 2020002938

3
Here, the record establishes that the Agency placed Complainant’s name on the Cautionary List in
March 2015 and Complainant initially contacted an EEO Counselor on February 11, 2019, which
is well beyond the 45-day time limit. On appeal, Complainant asserts that, while he first learned
that he was placed on the Cautionary L ist on or about November 1, 2018 , when he received the
report of investigation relating to an unrelated complaint, he did not understand the Cautionary
List’s meaning at that time. He further asserts that he did not become suspicious of the Agency’s
actions until December 15, 2018, when he received the report of investigation of a second unrelated
complaint. We find Complainant should reasonably have suspected discrimination on November
1, 2018, when he received the report of investigation indicating his name was on the Cautionary
List, which was more than 45 days prior to his initial contact with an EEO Counselor on February
11, 2019. Therefore, we find the dismissal for untimeliness was proper.

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal
decision.

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission) from the Agency's decision dated June 16, 2020, dismissing his complaint of
unlawful employment discrimination in violation of Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq., and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Co mplainant worked as a Police Officer at the
Agency’s Boston VA Medical Center facility in Boston, Massachusetts.

On April 29, 2020, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint alleging that the Agency subjected
him to discrimination on the bases of disability and age when, on April 11, 2020, he became aware
that he was not selected for the Security Assistant position, vacancy announcement number RS -
15-EER-1357517, on April 28, 2015.

The Agency dismissed the complaint, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2), for untimely EEO
counselor contact. The instant appeal followed.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2020004438

2
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.105(a)(1) requires that complaints of discrimination be
brought to the attention of the Equal Employment Opportunity Counselor within forty -five (45)
days of the date of the matter alleged to be discriminatory or, in the ca se of a personnel action,
within forty-five (45) days of the effective date of the action. The Commission has adopted a
“reasonable suspicion” standard (as opposed to a “supportive facts” standard) to determine when
the forty-five (45) day limitation period is triggered. See Howard v. Dep't of the Navy , EEOC
Request No. 05970852 (Feb. 11, 1999). Thus, the time limitation is not triggered until a
complainant reasonably suspects discrimination, but before all the facts that support a charge of
discrimination have become apparent. The time limitation is subject to waiver, estoppel and
equitable tolling pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(c).

In the instant case, the alleged discriminatory non-selection occurred on April 28, 2015. On appeal,
Complainant acknowledges that he first sought EEO counseling on April 13, 2020, nearly five
years later and well beyond the 45-day time limit.

However, Complainant argues that the facts of his case warrant equitable tolling. He asserts that,
in March 2015, the Agency , without his knowledge, added his name to a “Cautionary List” of
employees who left the Agency under unfavorable circumstances . He claims that he first learned
that he was placed on this list on or about November 1, 2018, when he received a report of
investigation in an unrelated EEO complaint. However, he asserts that his time limit for
challenging his 2015 non- selection should not be triggered until April 11, 2020, when he first
learned he was initially referred for consideration as qualified for the position and realized that his
placement on the Cautionary List was used against him with respect to the position.

We disagree with Complainant’s reasoning and find he should reasonably have suspected
discrimination on November 1, 2018, when he received the report of investigation indicating his
name had been on the Cautionary List since March 2015. Therefore, because he did not initiate
contact with an EEO Counselor until April 13, 2020, more than 45 days after November 1, 2018,
we find his complaint was untimely. We also find that Complainant has failed to provide sufficient
justification for extending or tolling the time limit.

Accordingly, the Agency's final decision dismissing Complainant's complaint is AFFIRMED.

DECISION

The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) accepts
Complainant’s appeal, pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s January 22, 2019
final decision concerning an equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint claiming
employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII),
as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Full-Time General Clerk, PS 6 at the
Agency’s Northern Virginia Processing and Distribution Center in Merrifield, Virginia.

On August 14, 2018, Complainant filed a formal EEO complaint claiming that she was subjected
to discriminatory harassment based on her disability (deaf) when:

1. Complainant’s assigned duties have been provided to her co-workers;

2. Complainant has been denied an interpreter;

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2019002501

2
3. on February 28, 2018, Complainant’s request to meet with the Senior Manager,
Distribution Operations (“DO Manager”) was denied; and

4. on March 7, 2018, and other dates, Complainant has been excluded from tour
conversations/meetings.

After the investigation of the claims,
2 the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of the right to request a hearing before an EEOC
Administrative Judge (AJ) or a final decision within thirty days of receipt of the correspondence.
Complainant did not respond.

On January 22, 2019, the Agency issued the instant final decision, pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), finding no discrimination.

The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant argues the Report of Investigation was
incomplete because it did not contain her affidavit, which she asserts she timely completed and
submitted. Complainant provides evidence that she mailed her affidavit by 2-day priority mail
on October 15, 2018. However, it appears her document was not delivered until November 20,
2018. Complainant provides a copy of her completed affidavit and attached documents.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Preliminary Matter – Submissions on Appeal

Here, the ROI indicates that Complainant failed to submit an affidavit during the investigation of
her complaint. Therefore, the Agency’s final decision was issued without consideration of
testimony for Complainant. On appeal, Complainant has demonstrated that she timely mailed
her affidavit to the Agency’s investigator. In accordance with instructions from the EEO
investigator, Complainant was required to mail her completed affidavit with a postmark date no
later than 15 days after she received the EEO investigator’s letter. The record reflects that
Complainant received the letter on October 15, 2018, and Complainant timely mailed her
affidavit on October 15, 2018. However, for circumstances beyond Complainant’s control, the
post office did not deliver her affidavit until November 20, 2018, almost one month after the
EEO investigator had transferred the ROI to the Agency.

2 The Report of Investigation (“ROI”) indicates that Complainant did not complete or submit an
affidavit. On September 29, 2018, the EEO investigator sent Complainant a letter instructing her
to complete an affidavit and to mail the document, postmarked no later than 15 days after receipt
of the notice. Delivery confirmation indicates that Complainant received the September 29,
2018 letter on October 1, 2018. The record indicates that the EEO investigator did not receive
Complainant’s submission by the deadline and the EEO investigator therefore concluded the
investigation and submitted a copy of the ROI to the Agency on October 31, 2018.

2019002501

3
Given these circumstances, we will consider the affidavit and supporting documents submitted
by Complainant on appeal in adjudicating this appeal.

In her affidavit, Complainant states that she has been deaf since birth and management was
aware of her condition since she became employed with the Agency in May 1982. However,
Complainant maintained that she is able to perform her job duties with reasonable
accommodation.

For claim 1, Complainant explains in her affidavit that the DO Manager assigned her duties to
her co-workers on March 7, 2018.

Complainant further states in her affidavit that she requested an interpreter on February 20, 2018,
but that the DO Manager denied her request. Complainant submits a copy of a 4:45 am February
20, 2018 email where the DO Manager asked her why a task was not completed. Complainant
also submits a handwritten document wherein she wrote, on February 20, 2018 at 5:28 am, “I can
explain everything through VRI.
3 I would like to explain what happened.” Complainant
contends that the DO Manager denied her request to use VRI to speak with him when he
responded, on February 20, 2018, to her message by writing, “Okay. In meantime I need it
done!!”

Complainant also submits a copy of a February 28, 2018 email she sent to the DO Manager
explaining that she had not heard from him since February 20, 2018, as to whether they would
meet via VRI. In the same email, Complainant requested to meet with the DO Manager to
explain what happened with her assignment. However, Complainant asserts that the DO
Manager denied this request. Complainant provides a copy of the DO Manager’s February 28,
2018 email where he stated, “I don’t need explanation. As long as it is done.”

Complainant clarifies in her affidavit that she was excluded from tour conversations and
meetings on February 20, 2018 and February 28, 2018 and she named the DO Manager as the
responsible management official.

Finally, Complainant contends that management was aware of her disability and her need for an
interpreter as a reasonable accommodation. Complainant explains that she had prior EEO
settlements in 1998, 1999, 2000, and 2002 that specified that management was required to
provide her with an interpreter for work-related needs. Additionally, Complainant disputes that
she ever submitted the Communication Accommodation Request Form provided in the record
which the Agency contends reflects that Complainant indicated that she did not need sign
language interpretation, written communication, a video phone, telephone headset, or an assistive
listening device.

3 VRI is an abbreviation for video remoter interpreting and is an alternate means of
communications for on-site interpreting services.

2019002501

4
Reasonable Accommodation – Claim 2 (Denial of Interpreter)

As previously discussed, Complainant is deaf and can complete the essential functions of her
duties with accommodation.
4 As stated on appeal, Complainant contends that she requested an
interpreter on February 20, 2018 but the DO Manager denied this request on February 28, 2018.

The DO Manager denied that he rejected Complainant’s request for an interpreter and explained
that he was unaware of Complainant being accommodated previously with an interpreter. We
also acknowledge Complainant’s statements on appeal that management had previously provided
her with interpreting services in 1998, 1999, 2000, and 2002. However, we note that there is no
recent documentation in the record to support Complainant’s reasonable accommodation needs
in 2018. The record contains a Communication Accommodation Request Form indicating that
Complainant is deaf, and she requested sign language interpretation only during training, a
captioned telephone to communicate on outside calls, and UbiDuo machine
5 to communicate
with employees in the office. Additionally, an October 6, 2017 letter indicates that the
Reasonable Accommodation Committee (“RAC”) was unable to process Complainant’s request
because Complainant failed to provide the requested medical documentation. Therefore, there is
no documentation in the record to support that Complainant ever complied the RAC’s request in
order for the Agency to make a determination on whether to grant Complainant’s reasonable
accommodation request.

Even if we presume, as Complainant contends, that the Agency agreed to provide Complainant
with an interpreter as a reasonable accommodation, we find that the record fails to demonstrate
that Complainant made a request for an interpreter on February 20, 2018. As Complainant asserts
on appeal, she requested to meet with the DO Manager to address his earlier concern about her
status on an assignment. Complainant stated in a February 20, 2018 handwritten note to the DO
Manager that she could explain through VRI what happened. However, by February 28, 2018,
the DO Manager emailed Complainant and informed her that he did not need an explanation.
Rather, the DO Manager indicated that he simply needed the task to be completed. In this
instance, we find that the essence of Complainant’s February 20, 2018 request was to have a
meeting with the DO Manager. Thus, Complainant’s request and subsequent need for VRI
services was contingent upon whether the DO Manager agreed to have a meeting to discuss her
assignment. The DO Manager denied the Complainant’s request to meet with him, and his
denial to have a meeting does not constitute as a denial of a reasonable accommodation.

Therefore, we find that Complainant has not shown that the Agency violated the Rehabilitation
Act by denying her a reasonable accommodation.

4 We presume for the purposes of analysis only, and without so finding, that Complainant is an
individual with a disability.

5 An UbiDuo machine is a communication device that allows a deaf person and a hearing person
to interact with each other.

2019002501

5
Harassment – Claims 1, 3, and 4

To establish a claim of discriminatory environment harassment, Complainant must show that: (1)
she belongs to a statutorily protected class; (2) she was subjected to harassment in the form of
unwelcome verbal or physical conduct involving the protected class; (3) the harassment
complained of was based on her statutorily protected class; (4) the harassment affected a term or
condition of employment and/or had the purpose or effect of unreasonably interfering with the
work environment and/or creating an intimidating, hostile, or offensive work environment; and
(5) there is a basis for imputing liability. See Henson v. City of Dundee, 682 F.2d 897 (11th Cir.
1982).

In other words, Complainant must establish that she was subjected to conduct that was either so
severe or so pervasive that a “reasonable person” in Complainant’s position would have found
the conduct to be hostile or abusive. Complainant must also prove that the conduct was taken
because of a protected basis – in this case, her disability. Only if Complainant establishes both
of those elements – hostility and motive – will the question of Agency liability present itself.

Upon review, we find that the Agency correctly determined that Complainant was not subjected
to discriminatory harassment.

Claim 1: Assignment of Complainant’s Duties to other Co-workers

On appeal, Complainant claimed that the DO Manager reassigned her duties to another co-
worker. In contrast, the DO Manager testified that he did not know what Complainant was
talking about. The DO Manager explained that he was not Complainant’s immediate supervisor
and Complainant did not work directly under him.

Claim 3: Denied February 28, 2018 Meeting

On appeal, Complainant stated that the DO Manager declined to meet with her on February 28,
2018.

The DO Manager testified that Complainant may have requested a meeting with him and if she
did, he likely referred her back to her immediate supervisor. The DO Manager clarified that he
had not denied any requests from employees, but he does make sure that all employees follow
the chain-of-command and contact their immediate manager first.

2019002501

6
Claim 4: Exclusion from Tour Conversations/Meetings

In her affidavit submitted on appeal, Complainant clarified that the DO Manager excluded her
from meetings on February 20, 2018 and February 28, 2018. However, the DO Manager denied
having any knowledge of this claim.

Considering these allegations, even if true, Complainant has not shown evidence that
considerations of her disability motivated management’s actions toward Complainant. Aside
from Complainant’s testimony, there is no other testimony in the record to support
Complainant’s claims. Additionally, the DO Manager denied having any knowledge of
excluding Complainant from meetings or reassigning Complainant’s duties to other co-workers.
The DO Manager clarified that he was not Complainant’s immediate supervisor and that he
directed all employees to follow the chain-of-command by contacting their immediate supervisor
first. Her claim of discriminatory harassment is precluded based on our findings that
Complainant failed to establish that any of the actions taken by the Agency were motivated by
her disability. See Oakley v. U.S. Postal Service, EEOC Appeal No. 01982923 (Sept. 21, 2000).

CONCLUSION

We AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision because the preponderance of the evidence of record
does not establish that discrimination occurred.

The record contains a copy of Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation reflecting that he received progress reviews on March 14, 2017, and July 7, 2017, and a final evaluation on October 1 7, 2017. The record reflects that Complainant initiated EEO contact on May 4, 2018, more than 90 days from when he received his final rating for his 2017 performance evaluatio n. Complainant does no t provide sufficient justification for extending the applicable time limit. Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final action implementing the EEOC AJ’s decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint.

Appeal No. 2020002182

Agency No. HS-USCG-02153-2019

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission) from the Agency's final decision dated January 8, 2020, dismissing a formal
complaint of unlawful employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
of 1964 (Title VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as an Attorney Advisor in Norfolk,
Virginia. On September 16, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency
subjected her to discrimination based on race (African-American).

In its final decision, dated January 8, 2020, the Agency determined that Complainant’s complaint
was comprised of the following claim:

On July 5, 2019, and again on August 14, 2019, Complainant became aware that
the Legal Service Command management hired a white female, as a G S-14
Attorney Advisor in the General Law Division in 2017, to perform the same duties
that Complainant was forced to perform as a GS -13 Attorney Advisor when she
worked at the same field office.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2020002182

2
The Agency dismissed the formal complaint on the grounds tha t Complainant previously raised
the same claim which is currently pending before the EEOC. The Agency reasoned that
Complainant previously raised this matter in a prior EEO complaint, Agency Case No. HS-USCG-
00420-2018 and is pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Specifically, the Agency
stated “[t]he record showed Complainant not only recited identical facts, but also implicated
identical responsible management officials with very slight exceptions.” Final Agency Decision
at 2.

The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant asserts that the Agency’s framing of her
claim does not fully capture all her issues. Specifically, Complainant states that “the elements of
the current complaint are not identical …[to] the matter pending before t he EEOC because the
[prior] complaint does not allege that the Agency used a fraudulent position description…as a basis
of discrimination…The use of the fraudulent position description as alleged in the signed statement
of [C1] was not investigated as part of [the prior complaint]…” Complainant also asserts that she
has named several individuals as responsible management officials that she did not name in the
prior complaint.

In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision dismissing Complainant’s
complaint. The Agency further asserts that the fact that C1 was unhappy with her assigned duties
is immaterial to either of her complaints.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

The regulation set forth at 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1) provides that the agency shall dismiss a
complaint that states the same claim that is pending before or has been decided by the agency or
Commission.

The Agency properly dismissed Complainant’s compla int for previously raising the same matter
which is currently pending before the Commission. Commission records reflect that Agency Case
No. HS-USCG-00420-2018 is currently pending before an EEOC AJ , EEOC Hearing No. 430-
2018-00358X. Commission records contain a copy of the Report of Investigation for Agency Case
No. HS-USCG-00420-2018. By letter dated January 16, 2018, the Agency accepted numerous
claims in her prior complaint. Specifically, the Agency accepted the following claim:

On November 29, 2017, Complainant became aware that she was compensated at
the GS-13 grade level for 5 years performing some of the same duties and had a
greater volume of work than the current female incumbent who was hired at the
GS-14 grade level.

The record contains a copy of an email from Complainant dated August 14, 2019 regarding
the instant formal complaint. Therein, Complainant stated:

[p]lease accept this notification as my request to be assigned an EEO Counselor
and my filing of an EEO complaint…on the basis of race (African American) when

 2020002182

3
on July 5, 2019, and again on August 14, 2019, I became aware that the Legal
Service Command management…hired a white female, (C1), as a GS-14 Attorney
Advisor…to perform the same duties that I was force d to perform as a G S-13
Attorney Advisor…[C1] explained that she is only responsible for civilian
personnel matters and that the position description was fraudulent because
according to the position description and the job announcement she was a general
law attorney required to handle real property, environmental law, ethics etc.

Based on the foregoing, we find that the crux of Complainant’s instant formal complaint is that she
was working in a position and being compensated at the GS -13 level while her white co -worker
(C1) was performing the same duties and being compensated at the GS-14 level and this is the same
matter previously raised in Agency Case No. HS -USCG-00420-2018. To the extent that
Complainant is alleging that her claim that C1 was in a fraudulent position description and that this
was not part of her prior complaint, the record reflects that Complainant did raise this matter in her
prior complaint. Complainant, in her affidavit for her prior complaint, stated that C1 informed
Complainant that she was hired as a GS-14 Attorney Advisor and that C1 feels that the command
lied about her position being a General Law position. Report of Investigation for Agency Case No.
HS-USCG-0420-2018 at 160.

We further find, however, that the matter of C1 allegedly being in a fraudulent position description
is background evidence to Complainant’s claim that she was not compensated at a GS -14 level
rather than a separate independent claim. Moreover, any cause of action regarding C1 al legedly
being placed under a “fraudulent position description,” would render C1 aggrieved rather than
Complainant. Finally, we do not find that Complainant including additional responsible
management officials in the instant complaint changes the substance of her claim.

Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final decision dismissing the formal complaint on the
grounds that she previously raised the same matter which is pending before the Commission.

STATEMENT OF RIGHTS - ON APPEAL

RECONSIDERATION (M0617)
The Commission may, in its discretion, reconsider the decision in this case if the Complainant or
the Agency submits a written request containing arguments or evidence which tend to establish
that:
1. The appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or
law; or
2. The appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or
operations of the Agency.
Requests to reconsider, with supporting statement or brief, must be filed with the Office of Federal
Operations (OFO) within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of this decision.

 2020002182

4
A party shall have twenty (20) calendar days of receipt of another party’s timely request for
reconsideration in which to submit a brief or statement in opposition. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405;
Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110),
at Chap. 9 § VII.B (Aug. 5, 2015). All requests and arguments must be submitted to the Director,
Office of Federal Operations, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Complainant’s
request may be submitted via regular mail to P.O. Box 77960, Washington, DC 20013, or by
certified mail to 131 M Street, NE, Washington, DC 20507. In the absence of a legible postmark,
the request to reconsider shall be deemed timely filed if it is received by mail within five days of
the expiration of the applicable filing period. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604. The agency’s request
must be submitted in digital format via the EEOC’s Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP). See 29
C.F.R. § 1614.403(g). The request or opposition must also include proof of service on the other
party.
Failure to file within the time period will result in dismissal of your request for reconsideration as
untimely, unless extenuating circumsta nces prevented the timely filing of the request. Any
supporting documentation must be submitted with your request for reconsideration. The
Commission will consider requests for reconsideration filed after the deadline only in very limited
circumstances. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(c).
COMPLAINANT’S RIGHT TO FILE A CIVIL ACTION (S0610)
You have the right to file a civil action in an appropriate United States District Court within ninety
(90) calendar days from the date that you receive this decision. If you file a civil action, you must
name as the defendant in the complaint the person who is the official Agency head or department
head, identifying that person by his or her full name and official title. Failure to do so may result
in the dismissal of your case in court. “Agency” or “department” means the national organization,
and not the local office, facility or department in which you work. If you file a request to reconsider
and also file a civil action, filing a civil action will terminate the administ rative processing of
your complaint.
RIGHT TO REQUEST COUNSEL (Z0815)
If you want to file a civil action but cannot pay the fees, costs, or security to do so, you may request
permission from the court to proceed with the civil action without paying these fees or costs.
Similarly, if you cannot afford an attorney to represent you in the civil action, you may request the
court to appoint an attorney for you. You must submit the requests for waiver of court costs or
appointment of an attorney directly to the court, not the Commission. The court has the sole
discretion to grant or deny these types of requests.

 2020002182

5
Such requests do not alter the time limits for filing a civil action (please read the paragraph titled
Complainant’s Right to File a Civil Action for the specific time limits).

Agency No. 200H-0523-2019101907

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission) from the Agency's decision dated February 13, 2020, dismissing his complaint of
unlawful employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title
VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.

BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant was a former Police Officer, GS-
7, at the Agency’s West Roxbury VA Medical Center (VAMC) facility in West Roxbury,
Massachusetts.

On March 15, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency subjected him
to unlawful retaliation for prior protected EEO activity when, on February 7, 2019, he was placed
on a cautionary list of employees who left the Agency under negative terms, including conduct
unbecoming.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2020002938

2
The Agency accepted the complaint and conducted an investigation which revealed the following
pertinent results.

Complainant was employed at the Agency from January 19, 2010 to February 3, 2013.

In March 2015, Complainant’s name was added to a “Cautionary List,” which was a list of former
employees known only to the Human Resources Division of the VA Boston Healthcare System
and prospective Agency employers.

On or about November 1, 2018, Complainant received a report of investigation for an unrelated
complaint indicating that he had been placed on the “Cautionary List” for former employees.

On December 15, 2018, Complainant submitted a request under the Freedom of Information Act
for a copy of the “Cautionary List that the VA Boston Healthcare Human Resources
Employee/Labor Relations keeps on file [which] documents former employees who left the facility
under negative terms including conduct unbecoming.”

On February 7, 2019, the Agency responded to Complainant’s request and provided a document
indicating Complainant’s name was on the Cautionary List.

On February 11, 2019, Complainant contacted an EEO Counselor regarding the instant complaint.

After its investigation into the complaint, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission) Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely
requested a hearing. The Agency submitted a Motion to D ismiss. The AJ subsequently issued a
Decision and Order dismissing the complaint pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(2), for untimely
EEO Counselor contact.

The Agency issued its final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal. The instant appeal followed.
 ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.105(a)(1) requires that complaints of discrimination be
brought to the attention of the Equal Employment Opportunity Counselor within forty-five (45)
days of the date of the matter alleged to be discriminatory or, in the case of a personnel action,
within forty-five (45) days of the effective date of the action. The Commission has adopted a
“reasonable suspicion” standard (as opposed to a “supportive facts” standard) to determine when
the forty-five (45) day limitation period is triggered. See Howard v. Dep't of the Navy, EEOC
Request No. 05970852 (Feb. 11, 1999). Thus, the time limitation is not triggered until a
complainant reasonably suspects discrimination, but before all the facts that support a charge of
discrimination have become apparent.

 2020002938

3
Here, the record establishes that the Agency placed Complainant’s name on the Cautionary List in
March 2015 and Complainant initially contacted an EEO Counselor on February 11, 2019, which
is well beyond the 45-day time limit. On appeal, Complainant asserts that, while he first learned
that he was placed on the Cautionary L ist on or about November 1, 2018 , when he received the
report of investigation relating to an unrelated complaint, he did not understand the Cautionary
List’s meaning at that time. He further asserts that he did not become suspicious of the Agency’s
actions until December 15, 2018, when he received the report of investigation of a second unrelated
complaint. We find Complainant should reasonably have suspected discrimination on November
1, 2018, when he received the report of investigation indicating his name was on the Cautionary
List, which was more than 45 days prior to his initial contact with an EEO Counselor on February
11, 2019. Therefore, we find the dismissal for untimeliness was proper.

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order adopting the AJ’s dismissal
decision.

STATEMENT OF RIGHTS - ON APPEAL
RECONSIDERATION (M0617)
The Commission may, in its discretion, reconsider the decision in this case if the Complainant or
the Agency submits a written request containing arguments or evidence which tend to establish
that:
1. The appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or
law; or
2. The appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or
operations of the Agency.
Requests to reconsider, with supporting statement or brief, must be filed with the Office of Federal
Operations (OFO) within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of this decision. A party shall have
twenty (20) calendar days of receipt of another party’s timely request for reconsideration in
which to submit a brief or statement in opposition. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405; Equal Employment
Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110), at Chap. 9 § VII.B
(Aug. 5, 2015). All requests and arguments must be submitted to the Director, Office of Federal
Operations, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission. Complainant’s request may be
submitted via regular mail to P.O. Box 77960, Washington, DC 20013, or by certified mail to 131
M Street, NE, Washington, DC 20507. In the absence of a legible postmark, the request to
reconsider shall be deemed timely filed if it is received by mail within five days of the expiration
of the applicable filing period. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604. The agency’s request must be submitted
in digital format via the EEOC’s Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP). See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.403(g). The request or opposition must also include proof of service on the other party.
Failure to file within the time period will result in dismissal of your request for reconsideration as
untimely, unless extenuating circumstances prevented the timely filing of the request.

 2020002938

4
Any supporting documentation must be submitted with your request for reconsideration. The
Commission will consider requests for reconsideration filed after the deadline only in very limited
circumstances. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.604(c).
COMPLAINANT’S RIGHT TO FILE A CIVIL ACTION (S0610)
You have the right to file a civil action in an appropriate United States District Court within ninety
(90) calendar days from the date that you receive this decision. If you file a civil action, you must
name as the defendant in the complaint the person who is the official Agency head or department
head, identifying that person by his or her full name and official title. Failure to do so may result
in the dismissal of your case in court. “Agency” or “department” means the national organization,
and not the local office, facility or department in which you work. If you file a request to reconsider
and also file a civil action, filing a civil action will terminate the administrative processing of
your complaint.
RIGHT TO REQUEST COUNSEL (Z0815)
If you want to file a civil action but cannot pay the fees, costs, or security to do so, you may request
permission from the court to proceed with the civil action without paying these fees or costs.
Similarly, if you cannot afford an attorney to represent you in the civil action, you may request the
court to appoint an attorney for you. You must submit the requests for waiver of court costs or
appointment of an attorney directly to the court, not the Commission. The court has the sole
discretion to grant or deny these types of requests. Such requests do not alter the time limits for
filing a civil action (please read the paragraph titled Complainant’s Right to File a Civil Action for
the specific time limits).

DECISION
Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission) from the Agency's final action d ated November 26, 2019, dismissing a formal
complaint of unlawful employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
of 1964 (Title VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq.
BACKGROUND
The record reflects the following chronology of events. During the relevant time period,
Complainant was an Electrician Supervisor at the Agency’s Portsmouth, Virginia facility.
Complainant filed an EEO complaint on August 30, 2018.
In a Corrected Partial Dismissal letter dated Marc h 15, 2019, the Agency determined that the
formal complaint was comprised of the following claims:
1. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race (African
American) and age by [a named management official] on April 17, 2018
when he received a negative performance evaluation.
1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

20200018412
2. Was [Complainant] discriminated against based on race, age, and reprisal
and subjected to a hostile work environment when he was not promoted to
Zone Manager, GS-2805-12.
The Agency accepted claim (1) for investigation. However, the Agency dismissed claim (2) on
procedural grounds. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 40-41. In a September 19, 2019 Order on
Initial Conference, the EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ) noted that Complainant does not contest
the dismissed claim. In addition, Complainant does not expressly contest the dismissed claim on
appeal. Thus, we decline to address the dismissed claim further herein.
Upon completion of the investigation, Complainant requested a hearing before an EEOC AJ.
On October 23, 2019, the EEOC AJ issued a decision dismissing Complainant’s complaint on
procedural grounds. To the extent that Complainan t was alleging that he was subjected to
discrimination based on the Agency’s April 17, 2018 mid-term progress review, the AJ dismissed
this matter for failure to state a claim and for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action. The
AJ further found that the crux of Complainant’s claim were the comments in his 2017 (rather than
2018) performance evaluation. To the extent Co mplainant was challenging his 2017 evaluation,
the EEOC AJ dismissed this claim for untimely EEO Counselor contact. The AJ reasoned that
Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation was dated October 17, 2017, for its final rating but
Complainant did not initiate EEO Counselor contact until May 4, 2018, outside of the applicable
time period.
On November 26, 2019, the Agency issued a final order implementing the AJ’s decision
dismissing Complainant’s complaint on procedural grounds.
Complainant does not submit a statement or brief on appeal.
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS
We find that to the extent Complainant alle ged discrimination based on his 2018 mid-year
evaluation, the Agency properly dismissed this matter for alleging a proposal to take a personnel
action. EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107 (a)(5) p rovides that an agency shall dismiss a
complaint that alleges that a proposal to take a personnel action, or other preliminary step to taking
a personnel action, is discriminatory. The Commissi on has held that a periodic progress review
does not create a personal harm. See Jackson v. Central Intelligence Agency, EEOC Request No.
05931177 (June 24, 1994).
In the instant matter, the EEO Counselor’s Repo rt lists April 2018 as the date of the alleged
discriminatory incident. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 17-18. The record reflects that a progress
review was issued to Complainant on April 17, 2018 and that Complainant refused to sign it. ROI
at 116. Because this claim involved an alleged di scriminatory progress review, we find that the
Agency properly dismissed this matter for alleging a proposal to take a personnel action.

20200018413
We concur with the AJ that the crux of Co mplainant’s claim is his 2017 (rather than 2018)
performance evaluation. The record contains a declaration under penalty from Complainant. ROI
at 56. Therein, Complainant expressly sets forth the negative comments that he received in an
evaluation which he alleges encompasses his claim. ROI at 58. The record reflects that these
comments were made in Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation. ROI at 117. Complainant
also lists in his declaration under penalty a named management official (Q1) who he alleges is the
responsible management official. ROI at 58. The record reflects that Q1 was the rating official in
Complainant’s 2017 performance evaluation and not his 2018 evaluation. ROI at 117, 64.
EEOC Regulation 29 C.F.R. § 1614.105(a)(1) requires that complaints of discrimination should
be brought to the attention of the Equal Employment Opportunity Counselor within forty-five (45)
days of the date of the matter al leged to be discriminatory or, in the case of a personnel action,
within forty-five (45) days of the effective date of the action. The Commission has adopted a
"reasonable suspicion" standard (as opposed to a "supportive facts" standard) to determine when
the forty-five (45) day limitation period is triggered. See Howard v. Dep’t of the Navy, EEOC
Request No. 05970852 (Feb. 11, 1999). Thus, th e time limitation is not triggered until a
complainant reasonably suspects discrimination, but before all the facts that support a charge of
discrimination have become apparent.
EEOC Regulations provide that the agency or the Commission shall extend the time limits when
the individual shows that he was not notified of the time limits and was not otherwise aware of
them, that he did not know and reasonably should not have known that the discriminatory matter
or personnel action occurred, that despite due diligence he was prevented by circumstances beyond
his control from contacting the Counselor within the time limits, or for other reasons considered
sufficient by the agency or the Commission.
We find that the AJ properly dismissed Comp lainant’s claim regarding his 2017 performance
evaluation for untimely EEO Counsel or contact. The record contains a copy of Complainant’s
2017 performance evaluation reflecting that he received progress reviews on March 14, 2017, and
July 7, 2017, and a final evaluation on October 1 7, 2017. ROI at 117. The record reflects that
Complainant initiated EEO contact on May 4, 2018, more than 45 days from when he received his
final rating for his 2017 performance evaluatio n. Complainant does no t provide sufficient
justification for extending the applicable time limit.
Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final action implementing the EEOC AJ’s decision
dismissing Complainant’s complaint.

DECISION

Complainant filed a timely appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC
or Commission) from the Agency's final decision dated January 8, 2020, dismissing a formal
complaint of unlawful employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act
of 1964 (Title VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq.

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked for the Agency as an Attorney Advisor in Norfolk,
Virginia. On September 16, 2019, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the Agency
subjected her to discrimination based on race (African-American).

In its final decision, dated January 8, 2020, the Agency determined that Complainant’s complaint
was comprised of the following claim:

On July 5, 2019, and again on August 14, 2019, Complainant became aware that
the Legal Service Command management hired a white female, as a G S-14
Attorney Advisor in the General Law Division in 2017, to perform the same duties
that Complainant was forced to perform as a GS -13 Attorney Advisor when she
worked at the same field office.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

 2020002182

2
The Agency dismissed the formal complaint on the grounds tha t Complainant previously raised
the same claim which is currently pending before the EEOC. The Agency reasoned that
Complainant previously raised this matter in a prior EEO complaint, Agency Case No. HS-USCG-
00420-2018 and is pending before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Specifically, the Agency
stated “[t]he record showed Complainant not only recited identical facts, but also implicated
identical responsible management officials with very slight exceptions.” Final Agency Decision
at 2.

The instant appeal followed. On appeal, Complainant asserts that the Agency’s framing of her
claim does not fully capture all her issues. Specifically, Complainant states that “the elements of
the current complaint are not identical …[to] the matter pending before t he EEOC because the
[prior] complaint does not allege that the Agency used a fraudulent position description…as a basis
of discrimination…The use of the fraudulent position description as alleged in the signed statement
of [C1] was not investigated as part of [the prior complaint]…” Complainant also asserts that she
has named several individuals as responsible management officials that she did not name in the
prior complaint.

In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final decision dismissing Complainant’s
complaint. The Agency further asserts that the fact that C1 was unhappy with her assigned duties
is immaterial to either of her complaints.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

The regulation set forth at 29 C.F.R. § 1614.107(a)(1) provides that the agency shall dismiss a
complaint that states the same claim that is pending before or has been decided by the agency or
Commission.

The Agency properly dismissed Complainant’s compla int for previously raising the same matter
which is currently pending before the Commission. Commission records reflect that Agency Case
No. HS-USCG-00420-2018 is currently pending before an EEOC AJ , EEOC Hearing No. 430-
2018-00358X. Commission records contain a copy of the Report of Investigation for Agency Case
No. HS-USCG-00420-2018. By letter dated January 16, 2018, the Agency accepted numerous
claims in her prior complaint. Specifically, the Agency accepted the following claim:

On November 29, 2017, Complainant became aware that she was compensated at
the GS-13 grade level for 5 years performing some of the same duties and had a
greater volume of work than the current female incumbent who was hired at the
GS-14 grade level.

The record contains a copy of an email from Complainant dated August 14, 2019 regarding
the instant formal complaint. Therein, Complainant stated:

[p]lease accept this notification as my request to be assigned an EEO Counselor
and my filing of an EEO complaint…on the basis of race (African American) when

3
on July 5, 2019, and again on August 14, 2019, I became aware that the Legal
Service Command management…hired a white female, (C1), as a GS-14 Attorney
Advisor…to perform the same duties that I was force d to perform as a G S-13
Attorney Advisor…[C1] explained that she is only responsible for civilian
personnel matters and that the position description was fraudulent because
according to the position description and the job announcement she was a general
law attorney required to handle real property, environmental law, ethics etc.
